right1: The burnt pan becoming new shows a clear before and after.
right2: The claim "It cleans anything" makes the sponge sound very powerful.
right3: Three sponges for £5 makes the product seem good value.
wrong1: The review "It cleans anything in seconds!" comes from a happy customer.
wrong2: A money-back guarantee at the end makes buying the sponges feel safe.
wrong3: The pan still looks old, so the claim seems honest.

statement: This billboard for Express Rail shows a fast silver train next to a busy road. On the road, hundreds of cars are not moving. The drivers look bored and angry. The train is full of people reading and relaxing. The slogan says, "London to Manchester in two hours." The billboard is next to a motorway, where drivers can see it.
right1: The stopped cars make driving look slow compared with the train.
right2: People reading and relaxing make the train journey seem easy.
right3: Placing the billboard by a motorway targets drivers stuck in traffic.
wrong1: The guarantee "London to Manchester in two hours" promises money back if late.
wrong2: A low ticket price shows the train is cheaper than driving.
wrong3: The happy, relaxed drivers make the road look better than the train.

statement: In the window of PhoneHub, there are product shots of three new phones in black, white and pink. Each phone has a price card under it. A big yellow sign says, "Free case with every phone!" A small picture shows the cases in different colours. Inside the shop, a young man in a green PhoneHub T-shirt is helping a customer.
right1: The free case makes buying a phone feel like getting something extra.
right2: Price cards under each phone help customers compare them quickly.
right3: The helpful worker inside makes the shop seem friendly and welcoming.
wrong1: Buy one get one free means every customer gets two new phones.
wrong2: The yellow sign offers a free phone with every case.
wrong3: The empty shop makes customers think the phones are not popular.

statement: This charity poster for Give Blood shows a nurse smiling at a young man. He is giving blood in a bright, clean room, and he looks calm and relaxed. The headline says, "You could save three lives." Under the photo, the poster claims that giving blood takes less than an hour. The website and phone number are at the bottom.
right1: The headline makes readers feel that they could save lives too.
right2: The calm young man shows that giving blood is not scary.
right3: Saying it takes less than an hour makes helping seem easy.
wrong1: The voiceover tells readers that giving blood is quick and easy.
wrong2: The poster says that giving blood takes about three hours.
wrong3: The nurse looks worried and serious, so giving blood seems dangerous.

statement: In this social media video, an influencer opens a free gift from a make-up brand called Lush Lips. She tries a bright red lipstick on camera. Her face shows surprise, then a big smile. She says, "I love this colour!" Under the video, a small line says, "Gift from Lush Lips." Many followers then ask where to buy the lipstick.
right1: Her surprised face, then big smile, makes her reaction seem real.
right2: Trying the lipstick on camera shows followers exactly how it looks.
right3: The line "Gift from Lush Lips" tells followers she got it free.
wrong1: The limited edition lipstick is only for her followers this week.
wrong2: A discount code under the video gives followers money off the lipstick.
wrong3: She looks disappointed with the colour, so followers trust her more.

statement: In this TV commercial for MealBox, a dad is cooking dinner. Smoke comes out of the pan, and the food is black. His children look at him and laugh. Then a MealBox arrives at the door. A voiceover says, "Even Dad can cook with MealBox." The family eat together, and the last shot is a product shot of the box.
right1: "Even Dad can cook" uses a stereotype that men cannot cook.
right2: The burnt food shows a problem that MealBox can solve.
right3: The family eating together shows a happy ending thanks to the box.
wrong1: The before and after review comes from a real, happy dad.
wrong2: The voiceover says, "Even Mum can cook," which uses a stereotype about women.
wrong3: The dad cooks perfectly from the start, so MealBox seems unnecessary.

statement: This poster for the Summer Sound festival shows a big crowd dancing in front of a stage at sunset. Coloured lights shine above them in the sky. At the top, the words "sponsored by Fizz" are in large yellow letters, with the Fizz logo. The poster lists the bands and the dates in July. Tickets cost £60 for the weekend.
right1: The large "sponsored by Fizz" words make the brand impossible to miss.
right2: The dancing crowd links Fizz with fun, music and summer.
right3: Sponsoring a festival helps Fizz reach young people who love music.
wrong1: Fizz is an influencer who tells festival fans what to drink.
wrong2: A free can of Fizz comes with every weekend ticket.
wrong3: The empty stage makes the festival look small and quiet.

statement: This online advert for ValueMart supermarket shows two boxes of cornflakes side by side. One is ValueMart's own brand, and the other is a famous competitor. The two boxes look almost exactly alike. Under them, the prices are £1.40 and £2.80. The headline says, "Same taste. Half the price." A green button at the bottom says, "Find your nearest store."
right1: Showing both prices makes ValueMart's cereal look like a bargain.
right2: The boxes look alike, so shoppers may think the cereal is the same.
right3: The button makes it easy to find a shop and buy.
wrong1: Buy one get one free means shoppers get two boxes for £1.40.
wrong2: Reviews from shoppers prove that the two cereals taste the same.
wrong3: The famous brand is cheaper, so ValueMart's cereal looks expensive.

statement: This radio advert for Snip hair salon is a conversation between two friends. One friend says, "I love your hair! Where did you go?" The other replies, "Snip, on the high street. It was so cheap!" Then a voiceover says that a haircut costs only £15 on weekdays. The advert ends with the salon's phone number and a short jingle.
right1: The friends' conversation sounds like a real recommendation, not an advert.
right2: "It was so cheap!" tells listeners the salon is good value.
right3: The voiceover gives the price clearly, so listeners know the cost.
wrong1: The product shot of her new hair makes listeners want the same cut.
wrong2: The voiceover says that a haircut costs only £15 at the weekend.
wrong3: The friend hates her new haircut, so the advert sounds honest.

statement: This magazine advert for Maison Noir shows a model holding a small black leather handbag. Her facial expression is serious, and she does not smile. The background is plain, bright white, so the bag stands out. Gold letters at the bottom say, "Only 100 made." There is no price and no other text, only the brand name at the top.
right1: The model's serious face makes the bag seem stylish and important.
right2: The words "Only 100 made" make the bag feel rare and special.
right3: The plain white background makes the black bag stand out.
wrong1: Buy one get one free shows that the bag is good value.
wrong2: The price at the bottom shows the bag is a luxury bargain.
wrong3: The model's big smile makes the bag feel cheap and friendly.

statement: This leaflet for Pronto Pizza has a photo of a large pepperoni pizza and a plate of hot garlic bread. The headline says, "Free garlic bread with every large pizza!" Under the photo, there is a short menu with prices. A large pizza costs only £11. The leaflet gives the phone number and says that delivery takes about thirty minutes.
right1: Free garlic bread makes customers feel they are getting something extra.
right2: The short menu with prices helps people decide and order quickly.
right3: Saying delivery takes thirty minutes makes ordering seem fast and easy.
wrong1: The limited edition pizza can only be ordered for thirty minutes.
wrong2: Reviews from customers on the leaflet make the pizza seem tasty.
wrong3: The small, dark photo makes the pizza look cold and old.

statement: This advert for Ripple trainers shows a teenage girl running through a rainy city at night. A close-up of her muddy shoes fills the bottom of the poster. The colours are dark blue and grey, but her trainers are bright orange, so they stand out. The slogan, "Nothing stops you", uses direct address to speak to the reader. Underneath, a call to action says, "Run today." The target audience is teenagers who never give up.
right1: The contrast between the orange trainers and the dark city draws attention to the product.
right2: The rain and mud suggest the trainers are tough enough for any running conditions.
right3: Using "you" in the slogan makes the reader feel the advert is speaking to them.
wrong1: The slogan uses a rhetorical question to make readers think about their own goals.
wrong2: The call to action creates urgency by telling readers the special offer ends today.
wrong3: The orange trainers blend into the dark background, so the girl seems part of the city.

statement: This charity advert on television begins in silence. A young boy in a dusty village walks for two hours to collect water, and the camera follows him in one long shot. Then a calm female voiceover quietly says, "Every day, millions of children make this journey." At the end, the screen turns white and shows the charity's logo and a website. The final line is an imperative: "Give £5 today and change one child's day."
right1: The long, silent walk makes viewers feel the boy's tiredness, which creates a strong emotional appeal.
right2: The voiceover's huge number shows that the problem is much bigger than one boy's story.
right3: The final imperative gives viewers one simple action and makes the cost seem small and possible.
wrong1: The final line is a rhetorical question that asks viewers what they would do in his place.
wrong2: The single long shot makes the journey feel quick, so the problem seems easy to solve.
wrong3: The calm voiceover is mainly aimed at children, who are the advert's most important target audience.

statement: In this sponsored post, a popular gaming influencer sits at her gaming desk wearing Echo headphones. She smiles at the camera and says, "I've tried every brand, and these are the best." Below the video, the caption reads, "Game louder. Win more. #EchoSquad". A small "Ad" label appears in the top corner. Many of the comments underneath ask where to buy them, and the influencer replies with a special discount code that ends on Friday.
right1: Her claim to have tried every brand is meant to make her opinion sound like an expert's.
right2: The hashtag invites followers to join a group, so buying the headphones feels like joining in.
right3: A discount code that ends on Friday creates urgency and pushes followers to buy quickly.
wrong1: The superlative "louder" in the caption claims these are the loudest headphones you can buy.
wrong2: Because the post has no label, many followers might not realise that it is really an advert.
wrong3: Her smile at the camera keeps a professional distance between the influencer and her followers.

statement: This billboard for Sunny Days orange juice looks like a faded old photograph. A family is having breakfast in a kitchen from the 1980s, with bright yellow walls, a striped tablecloth and an old radio on the table. The tagline says, "Tastes like it always did." In the bottom corner, there is a packshot of the carton next to fresh oranges. The small print explains that the juice now contains much less sugar than before.
right1: The 1980s kitchen creates nostalgia, reminding adult shoppers of happy breakfasts from their own childhood.
right2: The tagline suggests the brand has never changed, which may make it feel safe and trustworthy.
right3: Putting fresh oranges next to the carton links the product in our minds with natural, healthy fruit.
wrong1: The tagline uses alliteration so that shoppers remember the brand name when they are in a shop.
wrong2: The small print admits the juice has more sugar now, so the advert quietly hides a weakness.
wrong3: The radio on the table plays the brand's jingle, which helps people remember the advert later.

statement: In this online advert for the LingoLeap app, a teenage boy stands in a café in Madrid. In the first scene, he points nervously at the menu and looks confused and embarrassed. Then the words "Thirty days later" appear, and he orders confidently in Spanish while the waiter laughs at his joke. A voiceover asks, "What could you say in thirty days?" The advert ends with the app's logo and a green "Download free" button.
right1: The before and after scenes show the app's benefit in a way that viewers understand immediately.
right2: The voiceover's rhetorical question encourages viewers to imagine their own progress after thirty days.
right3: The waiter's laugh suggests the app helps people make real connections, not just order food.
wrong1: His confident ordering in the first scene shows that the app works from the very first day.
wrong2: The voiceover's imperative tells viewers exactly what they need to do next to start learning.
wrong3: The advert creates urgency by warning viewers that the free download ends at midnight tonight.

statement: This magazine advert for Aurum watches is printed mostly in black and gold. A man in a dark, expensive suit stands alone on the deck of a yacht at sunset, checking the time. His face is partly in shadow, but the watch is lit clearly. There is only one line of text: "For those who arrive." The brand name appears in small gold letters at the bottom of the page, and there is no price.
right1: The yacht and the suit make the watch aspirational by linking it with a wealthy lifestyle.
right2: Lighting the watch more clearly than the man's face makes the product the real focus.
right3: Leaving out the price suggests the watch is exclusive, for people who never need to ask.
wrong1: The detailed text explains the watch's features, giving readers sensible, practical reasons to buy it.
wrong2: The man's clear, smiling face invites readers to trust him as if he were a friend.
wrong3: The tagline works as a call to action, telling readers to go and buy the watch today.

statement: This public service advert on television shows a teenage boy walking home from school alone. He is looking down at his phone and smiling at a message. He steps onto the road without looking. Suddenly, we hear brakes screaming, and the screen goes black. There is silence for three seconds. Then white words appear: "Look up. It only takes a second." The advert was made by the city council and is shown before evening films.
right1: The sudden silence and black screen shock viewers into imagining what happened next.
right2: The imperative "Look up" gives teenagers one clear and simple action to remember.
right3: Showing it before evening films reaches young people when they are paying attention.
wrong1: The rhetorical question at the end makes viewers think about their own phone use.
wrong2: The final words, "It only takes a minute," suggest the danger is slow.
wrong3: The loud music during the crash makes the scene feel exciting, like an action film.

statement: This billboard for Pip's Pies shows a large golden pie on an old wooden kitchen table. Steam is rising from the pie, and a large piece has been cut out so we can see the chicken and mushroom filling inside. The colour palette is warm: brown, orange and cream. The tagline, in big hand-written letters, says, "Pie-fect for lunch." Underneath, a much smaller line says that the pies are baked fresh every morning in Yorkshire.
right1: The pun "Pie-fect" makes the tagline playful and easy for people to remember.
right2: The warm colour palette of brown, orange and cream gives the pie a homely feel.
right3: Cutting out a piece lets viewers see the filling, which makes the pie look generous.
wrong1: The rhetorical question in the tagline invites readers to think about their lunch.
wrong2: The small print offers a special discount for anyone who buys two pies today.
wrong3: The cold blue colour palette makes the pie seem fresh, light and healthy.

statement: In a popular action film, the hero has just escaped from a burning building. He sits on the back of an ambulance, tired and covered in dust. A paramedic hands him a cold can of Volt cola. He drinks it slowly, and the red label faces the camera for several seconds. The actor is one of the most famous stars in the world. The brand name is never spoken, and there is no advert break.
right1: This is product placement, because the cola appears inside the film, not in an advert break.
right2: Linking the drink with a tired hero suggests it brings relief after a hard moment.
right3: Using one of the world's most famous actors gives the cola a powerful, exciting brand image.
wrong1: This is a sponsored post, so the actor must tell viewers that he was paid.
wrong2: The hero says the brand name clearly, so viewers will remember it in the shop.
wrong3: The label is hidden from the camera, so viewers hardly notice which drink it is.

statement: This social media campaign for Dash trainers began with a short video of a famous dancer. She performs a simple dance in a car park wearing white Dash trainers, then says, "Your turn. #DanceWithDash." Within a week, thousands of teenagers had copied the dance and posted their own videos with the hashtag. Many of them wear Dash trainers too. The original video has been watched forty million times, and news websites have written about it.
right1: The hashtag gives teenagers an easy way to join in and share their own videos.
right2: Thousands of copies create a bandwagon effect, so more teenagers want to take part.
right3: The campaign went viral, so news websites gave the brand free extra attention as well.
wrong1: The dancer's testimonial explains in detail why Dash trainers are better than other brands.
wrong2: The video ends with the price and a discount code, which creates urgency.
wrong3: Because only a few people copied the dance, the trainers feel rare and exclusive.

statement: This magazine advert for Serene face cream shows a close-up of a woman's face. Her skin looks perfect, with no lines, spots or shadows. She is looking calmly at the reader. Next to her, a white jar sits on a smooth, flat grey stone. The headline says, "Our most advanced cream ever." At the bottom of the page, in very small print, are the words "Results may vary. Based on a study of 40 women."
right1: The perfect skin with no lines is idealised, so few readers could really look like that.
right2: The superlative "most advanced" makes the cream sound better than every cream before it.
right3: The small print about forty women shows the result may not be true for everyone.
wrong1: The rhetorical question in the headline makes readers wonder if their skin is good enough.
wrong2: The small print says the study was based on four thousand women, so the claim seems strong.
wrong3: The smooth grey stone and white jar give the advert a busy, colourful feel.

statement: This TV advert is part of a new campaign for Brew coffee. It shows different people on a busy weekday morning: a nurse finishing a night shift, a student late for a lecture, and a builder on a cold, windy roof. Each person drinks a cup of Brew and says the same two words: "Wake up." At the end, the tagline appears: "Brew. Wake up to more." The advert is shown early in the morning.
right1: Repeating "Wake up" with different people makes the tagline stick in viewers' minds.
right2: Showing a nurse, a student and a builder suggests Brew is for all kinds of workers.
right3: Showing it early in the morning reaches viewers just when they need coffee most.
wrong1: The alliteration in "Wake up to more" repeats the same sound at the start of each word.
wrong2: Showing a doctor, a teacher and a chef suggests Brew is mainly for professional workers.
wrong3: The people all look relaxed and well rested, so the coffee seems like a treat.

statement: This online advert appears at the bottom of a news article. It shows a photo of a smiling woman holding up an old pair of very large jeans. The headline says, "Doctors hate this one simple trick!" When readers click on it, they arrive at a page selling SlimLeaf tea. The page uses words like "miracle" and "shocking". In grey letters at the bottom, it says the tea should be used with diet and exercise.
right1: The headline is clickbait, because it promises a secret just to make readers click.
right2: Emotive words like "miracle" and "shocking" make the tea sound more exciting than it is.
right3: The grey line about diet and exercise suggests the tea may be misleading on its own.
wrong1: The doctor's testimonial gives the tea a serious, medical reason for readers to trust it.
wrong2: A countdown timer on the page creates urgency, so readers buy before they think.
wrong3: The calm, careful word choice makes the tea sound honest, scientific and safe.

statement: This radio advert for Fairway Bank begins with the sound of coins dropping into a glass jar. A calm, friendly voiceover says, "Do you want to save for something special?" She explains that young people can open a savings account with just one pound. Then she says the bank's new slogan slowly and clearly: "Save smart, spend safe." Soft guitar music plays quietly in the background, and the advert ends with the bank's website address.
right1: The alliteration in "Save smart, spend safe" makes the slogan easy for listeners to remember.
right2: The rhetorical question uses direct address to make listeners think about their own plans.
right3: Opening an account with one pound makes saving seem possible for young people.
wrong1: The superlative "smart" suggests Fairway is the cleverest bank for young people to choose.
wrong2: Urgency is created because the voiceover says the special offer ends this Friday.
wrong3: The loud, fast voiceover makes saving money sound stressful, difficult and a little frightening.

statement: This bag of Kale Kick crisps is bright green, with a drawing of fresh, dark kale leaves on the front. Big white letters across the top say, "The healthiest crisp in Britain." Under these words, there is a packshot of the crisps in a simple wooden bowl. Words such as "natural", "fresh" and "goodness" appear on the back of the bag. The nutrition table on the side shows that each small bag contains 150 calories.
right1: The superlative "healthiest" makes a strong claim that the crisps are better than all others.
right2: Words like "natural" and "fresh" have positive connotations that link the crisps with health.
right3: The green bag and kale leaves suggest the crisps are good for you.
wrong1: The imperative on the front tells shoppers to eat kale every single day.
wrong2: The packshot shows the crisps in a plastic bag, which makes them look cheap and ordinary.
wrong3: The nutrition table proves the crisps are healthier than every other brand in Britain.

statement: This Christmas advert for Hollins supermarket begins with an old man looking out of a window at the falling snow. He is alone, holding an old photo of his family. Then, suddenly, the doorbell rings. His daughter and grandchildren are standing outside, holding bags of food from Hollins. Slow piano music plays as they hug him and cook a big dinner together. At the end, the tagline appears in gold: "Christmas is better together. Hollins."
right1: The lonely old man creates an emotional appeal, so viewers feel sad and then relieved.
right2: Slow piano music makes the reunion feel warm, gentle and full of emotion.
right3: The tagline links Hollins with family, not just with buying food for Christmas.
wrong1: The superlative in the tagline claims Hollins is the best supermarket for Christmas food.
wrong2: Prices on the shopping bags show that Hollins is cheaper than other supermarkets.
wrong3: The family arrives with Hollins bags, but the old man prefers to stay alone.

statement: This poster for Comfy Step shoes shows a nurse in a blue uniform standing in a hospital corridor. She is smiling and pointing at her new white shoes. Next to her, there is a quote in large letters: "Twelve hours on my feet, and no pain." Under the quote, it says, "Sarah, nurse, Manchester." At the bottom, the poster asks, "Are you on your feet all day?" The poster appears in hospitals and train stations.
right1: Sarah's testimonial makes the claim about comfort feel believable, because it comes from a nurse.
right2: The rhetorical question uses direct address to speak to people who stand all day.
right3: Placing the poster in hospitals reaches the target market of nurses and doctors.
wrong1: The celebrity endorsement from Sarah works because she is a famous television star.
wrong2: The poster creates urgency by saying the shoes are half price until Friday.
wrong3: Sarah looks tired and her feet hurt, which makes the advert feel more honest.

statement: At the checkout in this supermarket, there is a long shelf of sweets and chocolate bars right beside the till. The packets are bright red, yellow and purple, and they are at the height of a small child's eyes. Some packets have famous cartoon characters from children's films on them. A small sign above the shelf says, "Treat yourself!" Everything costs less than a pound. While their parents pay, many children pick up a packet.
right1: Putting sweets beside the till encourages impulse buys while parents are busy paying for shopping.
right2: Placing packets at a child's eye level targets children, who then ask their parents.
right3: The bright colour palette of red, yellow and purple makes the packets eye-catching.
wrong1: The rhetorical question "Treat yourself!" makes children stop and think about what they want.
wrong2: A countdown on the sign creates urgency, so shoppers buy the sweets quickly.
wrong3: The high shelf keeps the sweets away from children, so only adults notice them.

statement: This billboard for the Vista family car shows a mother, a father and two young children driving along a quiet country road towards a lake. The sun is rising, and the sky is pink and gold. The children are laughing in the back seat, and a happy dog has its head out of the window. The car is clean, shiny and silver. The tagline says, "More room for what matters." The price begins at £24,000.
right1: The happy family scene is aspirational, showing a life many parents would like.
right2: The tagline suggests the car's space is for family and love, not just luggage.
right3: The sunrise colours of pink and gold make the trip feel fresh and hopeful.
wrong1: The pun in "More room for what matters" plays on two meanings of "Vista".
wrong2: The small print under the price explains that the car comes with free insurance.
wrong3: The empty road and lonely driver suggest the car is for people who like being alone.

statement: In this sponsored post, a beauty influencer with long, curly hair sits in front of a ring light. She holds up a small green bottle of Kiwi hair oil and says, "I've used this every day for six months, and look at my curls!" She runs her fingers through her hair. The caption says, "#ad Kiwi changed my hair routine. Link in my bio for 20% off." Her post has 300,000 likes and many comments.
right1: The "#ad" in the caption shows honestly that this is a paid, sponsored post.
right2: Her claim about using it every day for six months makes the endorsement sound real.
right3: The 20% discount and link work as a call to action for her followers.
wrong1: Her quote "look at my curls!" is a superlative that makes her hair sound the best.
wrong2: A countdown in the caption creates urgency, because the discount ends tonight.
wrong3: The influencer hides that she was paid, so followers may think the post is honest.

statement: This TV advert for Edge razors takes place in a dark bathroom with steel-grey walls. A tall, muscular man with no shirt shaves in front of a mirror. The music is loud and fast, with heavy drums. Each time he moves the razor, there is a sound like a sword. A deep male voiceover says, "Edge. The sharpest shave a man can get." The advert finishes with a packshot of the black and silver razor.
right1: The dark steel-grey colour palette gives the razor a hard, masculine brand image.
right2: The sword sound has connotations of strength and sharpness, like a weapon in battle.
right3: The superlative "sharpest" makes the razor sound better than any other on sale.
wrong1: The tagline is a call to action that tells men exactly where to buy it.
wrong2: The voiceover says, "The sharpest shave a woman can get," so the target market is women.
wrong3: The soft, gentle music and bright bathroom make shaving seem calm and relaxing.

statement: This poster for the Quit Now campaign shows a pair of human lungs on a plain white background. The lungs are grey and black, and they look damaged and dry. Above them, a headline in red capital letters says, "This is what smoking does." At the bottom, the poster says, "Stop today. Call our free, friendly helpline." The campaign is run by the government, and the posters appear in bus stops and doctors' waiting rooms.
right1: The grey, damaged lungs shock viewers, so the harm of smoking feels real and frightening.
right2: Red capital letters in the headline make the message feel urgent and serious.
right3: The imperative "Stop today" gives smokers a clear action and a free helpline to call.
wrong1: The rhetorical question in the headline asks smokers what they think smoking does.
wrong2: A testimonial from a former smoker explains how hard it was to quit.
wrong3: The colourful, friendly design makes the poster feel light and easy to ignore.

statement: This online advert for SkyHop appears when someone searches for flights to Rome. It shows a photo of a sunny square with an old stone fountain. Red letters flash at the top: "Only 3 seats left at this price!" Below, the price says, "Rome from £59." A large, bright orange button says, "Book now." In small grey print under the button, the advert says that bags cost extra and that prices change every few hours.
right1: "Only 3 seats left" creates urgency, so people feel they must book straight away.
right2: The sunny square and old stone fountain make Rome look relaxing and attractive.
right3: The small print about bags suggests the £59 price may be a little misleading.
wrong1: The superlative "Rome from £59" claims SkyHop is the cheapest airline in Europe.
wrong2: A testimonial from a happy traveller makes the airline seem friendly and reliable.
wrong3: The prices stay the same all week, so travellers can take their time to decide.

statement: This TV advert for Volley sportswear shows a famous tennis player during the final point of a big match. Everything happens in slow motion: the ball, the sweat on her face, and the crowd jumping up. She wins and falls slowly to her knees. The camera moves closer to the Volley logo on her shirt. Then the slogan appears in white letters on a black screen: "Never stop." There is no voiceover, only the crowd.
right1: Slow motion makes the final point and her win feel dramatic, emotional and important.
right2: The camera moving closer to the logo links Volley with victory and success.
right3: Using a famous tennis player is a celebrity endorsement that makes the brand aspirational.
wrong1: The rhetorical question "Never stop" encourages viewers to think about their own sporting goals.
wrong2: The voiceover explains how the clothes keep players cool and dry during long matches.
wrong3: Because she loses the match, the advert shows that trying hard is what matters.

statement: This poster for the Pixel Retro games console looks like an old video game from the 1990s. The pictures are made of big, square pixels, and the colours are bright purple and green. A small cartoon character jumps over a mushroom. The headline asks, "Remember 1995?" Underneath, the poster says that the console has fifty classic games inside. The posters appear in train stations at rush hour, where most travellers are adults going to work.
right1: The pixel graphics create nostalgia for adults who played games in the 1990s.
right2: The rhetorical question "Remember 1995?" invites adult readers to think back to their childhood.
right3: Placing posters in stations at rush hour reaches the target market of working adults.
wrong1: The alliteration in "Remember 1995?" makes the headline catchy and easy for readers to remember.
wrong2: Placing the posters in school playgrounds reaches the target market of young children.
wrong3: The modern, realistic graphics show that the console has the newest and most advanced technology.

statement: This magazine advert for Bean There coffee shows a small brown paper loyalty card on a café table. Nine of the ten circles on the card have been stamped with a coffee cup. Next to the card, there is a cup of coffee with a heart drawn in the milk. The headline says, "Your tenth coffee is on us." At the bottom, the advert says, "Pick up your card in any Bean There café today."
right1: The loyalty card rewards customers for coming back again and again, which builds brand loyalty.
right2: Showing nine stamps already filled makes the free tenth coffee feel very close.
right3: "Your tenth coffee" uses direct address, so readers imagine it is their own card.
wrong1: The superlative "tenth" shows that Bean There has the best coffee in town.
wrong2: The small print explains that the free coffee is only available on Mondays.
wrong3: The empty card suggests customers must buy many coffees before getting anything free.

statement: This poster at a bus stop is for Frosty ice lollies. It shows a packshot of three lollies, orange, pink and blue, sitting in a pile of ice. Drops of water run down them. The headline says, "Meltdown Monday: two for one, today only!" The poster has a timer in the corner, and it only appears on Mondays when the temperature is over twenty-five degrees. A small map at the bottom shows the nearest shop.
right1: The drops of water and ice make the lollies look cold on a hot day.
right2: Showing the poster only on hot Mondays reaches people when they really want a lolly.
right3: "Today only" and the timer create urgency, so people buy before it ends.
wrong1: The superlative "Meltdown Monday" says these are the coldest lollies in the shop.
wrong2: The headline "Two for one, all summer long" means there is no need to hurry.
wrong3: The poster appears on cold days, so the lollies seem like a winter treat.

statement: This TV advert for the Volta electric car shows a woman driving on a long, empty road through the desert. She stops at a small charging station in the middle of nowhere, next to a café. While her car charges, she buys a coffee. Before she finishes it, a sound tells her the car is ready. Then the tagline appears: "Fully charged in ten minutes." The final shot shows the car driving into the sunset.
right1: The tagline's clear number is the unique selling point that makes Volta different.
right2: Charging before she finishes a coffee shows the claim instead of only saying it.
right3: The empty desert road suggests the car can take you far from towns.
wrong1: The rhetorical question "Fully charged in ten minutes?" makes viewers doubt other electric cars.
wrong2: The small print explains that ten minutes is only possible at special stations.
wrong3: She waits a long time for the car to charge, so the advert feels honest.

statement: This advert appears on a popular food delivery app used by students in Shanghai. It is for ChaCha bubble tea. At the top, there is a photo of two tall cups of brown sugar milk tea with ice. Red Chinese and English words say, "Second cup ¥1, today only!" Under the photo, there is the hashtag #ChaChaTime and a small timer showing how many hours are left. A big, round red button says, "Order now."
right1: "Second cup ¥1" makes buying for a friend feel like a very good deal.
right2: The timer and "today only" create urgency, so students order straight away without thinking.
right3: Appearing on a delivery app reaches students when they are already choosing food.
wrong1: The imperative in the hashtag #ChaChaTime tells students exactly what to do next.
wrong2: The offer gives a free third cup, so it suits large groups of friends.
wrong3: The offer lasts all month, so students can wait and order whenever they like.

statement: This poster for the Clean Streets campaign shows a city pavement covered in rubbish: drink cans, crisp packets and coffee cups. In the middle of the poster, there is a clean green bin. Large black letters say, "Bin it. Don't drop it." Under this, smaller letters say, "Bin it for your street. Bin it for your city." The poster was made by the local council for this summer and appears in parks and shopping streets.
right1: The imperatives "Bin it" and "Don't drop it" give people a clear and simple instruction.
right2: Repeating the words "Bin it" several times makes the campaign's message easy to remember.
right3: The clean green bin contrasts with the rubbish, showing what people should choose.
wrong1: The rhetorical question "Don't drop it" makes readers think about their own rubbish.
wrong2: The poster was made by a drinks company, so it also advertises its cans.
wrong3: The clean, empty pavement shows that the city has no problem with rubbish.

statement: This TV advert for Swift swimwear shows an Olympic swimmer training alone in an empty pool before sunrise. The water is very still, and the only light comes from the pool. She dives in and swims very fast. When she stops, the camera shows the Swift logo on her swimming cap. A voiceover says, "Swift is proud to sponsor Team GB." The advert ends with a website where viewers can buy the same blue swimsuit.
right1: Sponsoring Team GB links the Swift brand with Olympic success and national pride.
right2: Training alone in an empty pool before sunrise makes the swimmer look determined.
right3: Showing the logo on her cap links the brand with an aspirational athlete.
wrong1: The swimmer's testimonial explains in detail why Swift swimsuits help her swim faster.
wrong2: A discount for viewers who buy the same swimsuit today creates a sense of urgency.
wrong3: The crowded, noisy pool makes swimming look fun and relaxed rather than serious.

statement: This online advert for the mobile game Kingdom Clash shows a huge battle between two cartoon armies. Giant dragons fly above the castles, and orange fire lights up the sky. Big gold letters say, "10 million players can't be wrong." Underneath, the advert shows that the game has 4.8 stars from over a million reviews. A green button says, "Download free and join the battle." The advert appears inside other games and on video websites.
right1: "10 million players can't be wrong" uses the bandwagon effect to persuade new players.
right2: The 4.8 stars from over a million reviews make the game seem trusted.
right3: The call to action "Download free and join the battle" makes starting feel easy.
wrong1: The superlative "10 million" says Kingdom Clash is the most exciting game ever.
wrong2: The game's low rating of 2.8 stars makes the bandwagon claim seem less believable.
wrong3: The calm, peaceful castles suggest the game is slow and relaxing to play.

statement: This magazine advert for the Azure Bay resort shows an empty beach with white sand and turquoise sea. A single wooden chair sits under a tall palm tree, facing the water. There are no people in the photo. The colour palette is white, turquoise and pale gold. Across the sky, elegant gold letters say, "Your escape is waiting." At the bottom, a small line gives the resort's website and the words "Seven nights from £1,200."
right1: "Your escape is waiting" uses direct address, so readers imagine themselves being there.
right2: The white, turquoise and gold colour palette makes the resort look calm and expensive.
right3: The single empty chair suggests peace and space away from busy everyday life.
wrong1: The imperative "Your escape is waiting" orders readers to go and book a holiday.
wrong2: Testimonials from happy guests at the bottom make the resort seem friendly and trustworthy.
wrong3: The crowded beach suggests the resort is lively and popular with young families.

statement: This billboard for the Wave mobile network shows a map of the whole country covered in bright blue. In front of the map, a young man is making a video call to his family from the top of a mountain. The headline says, "100% coverage*". Next to the star, at the bottom of the billboard, very small print explains that the figure is for towns and cities only. The billboard stands beside a busy road.
right1: The asterisk sends readers to small print that makes the headline less impressive.
right2: The claim "100% coverage" is misleading, because it is only true in towns and cities.
right3: The man calling from a mountain suggests the network works even in remote places.
wrong1: The superlative "100% coverage" says Wave is the cheapest mobile network in the country.
wrong2: The man is calling from a crowded city street, which shows the network works in busy places.
wrong3: The small print shows the network is even better than the headline says.

statement: This TV advert for Starla dolls takes place in a pink bedroom with pink curtains and a pink carpet. Three girls sit on the bed, brushing the long blonde hair of their dolls and choosing sparkly dresses and shoes for them. A soft, sweet song plays: "Starla, Starla, pretty as a star." At the end, all the girls hold up their dolls and smile sweetly. The advert is shown during children's programmes on Saturday morning.
right1: The all-pink bedroom uses a gender stereotype that girls only like pink things.
right2: Brushing hair and choosing dresses suggests girls should care most about how things look.
right3: Showing the advert during children's programmes on Saturday morning reaches young girls directly.
wrong1: The alliteration in "pretty as a star" repeats the same sound to sound sweet.
wrong2: A celebrity endorsement from a famous singer makes the dolls seem grown-up and cool.
wrong3: Boys and girls play together in the advert, so it challenges gender stereotypes.

statement: This charity poster for Shelter Now shows a man sleeping in a shop doorway at night. He is wrapped in an old grey blanket, and his shoes are next to him. In the photo, the legs of busy shoppers walk past him, but nobody stops or looks down. A white question appears in the middle: "Would you walk past?" At the bottom, it says, "£10 gives someone a warm bed tonight. Text BED to 70070."
right1: The rhetorical question makes readers ask themselves whether they would stop and help.
right2: The shoppers' legs walking past show how easy it is to ignore people.
right3: The call to action makes helping very simple: just a text message and £10.
wrong1: The imperative "Would you walk past?" orders readers to stop and give money.
wrong2: A testimonial from the man explains how he lost his home last winter.
wrong3: Shoppers stop to talk to the man, so the city seems kind and caring.

statement: This box of Hearth granola has a hand-drawn picture of a small farm on the front. There is a red barn, a field of ripe wheat, a few chickens and a farmer's kitchen with an open window. The words "homemade" and "golden" appear in brown, hand-written letters. On the back, there is a short story about the farmer's grandmother and her original recipe. The box is made of plain brown card, and it costs £4.50.
right1: The hand-drawn farm creates nostalgia for a simpler, old-fashioned way of country life.
right2: The word "homemade" has connotations of care and quality, not a big factory.
right3: The story of the grandmother's recipe makes the brand feel traditional and personal.
wrong1: The superlative "golden" claims that Hearth is the best granola you can buy.
wrong2: The story on the back describes a modern factory that makes thousands of boxes a day.
wrong3: The shiny plastic box and modern design make the granola look high-tech and new.

statement: This TV advert for Loyal dog food begins with a young boy getting a small puppy for his birthday. Then we watch the boy and the dog grow up together: playing in the garden, going to school, and later sitting together on the sofa. At the end, the man is grown up, and the dog is old and grey. The tagline says, "Loyal. Fifteen years of friendship." The advert has no words until the end.
right1: Watching the boy and dog grow old together creates a strong emotional appeal.
right2: The tagline links the brand name with loyalty between owners and their pets.
right3: "Fifteen years" suggests owners will stay with the brand for the dog's whole life.
wrong1: The rhetorical question in the tagline makes owners wonder how long their dog will live.
wrong2: A vet's testimonial explains why the food helps dogs live longer and healthier lives.
wrong3: The fast, funny voiceover all the way through keeps the advert light and cheerful.

statement: This online video for Surge energy drink shows a cyclist riding at full speed across the roof of a tall building. He jumps across the gap to another roof, lands safely, and keeps going without stopping. The video looks like it was filmed on a phone, and it has no music. At the end, he opens a can of Surge. It was posted with #SurgeOn, and it was shared millions of times in two days.
right1: The dangerous jump makes the video exciting enough to share, so it went viral.
right2: Filming on a phone makes it look real, not like a normal advert.
right3: The hashtag #SurgeOn helps people find the video and share it with friends online.
wrong1: The video is a testimonial in which the cyclist explains why he drinks Surge.
wrong2: The small print warns that the stunt was done by a professional with safety ropes.
wrong3: Calm music and a careful ride make the drink seem relaxing and safe.

statement: This poster for Northgate University shows five smiling students sitting on the grass in front of an old stone building. They come from many different countries, and they are laughing together at something on a phone. One is holding a laptop, and another is holding a cup of coffee. The headline says, "Your future starts here." At the bottom, the poster gives the date of the next open day and says, "Find your course today."
right1: "Your future starts here" uses direct address to speak to each young reader personally.
right2: Students from many different countries show that the university welcomes a wide demographic.
right3: The old stone building suggests the university has history and a good reputation.
wrong1: The rhetorical question "Your future starts here" makes readers doubt their own future plans.
wrong2: The small print lists the fees, so readers know the courses are good value.
wrong3: The serious, silent students in the photo suggest the university is strict and hard-working.

statement: This online advert for PriceRight supermarket shows a full shopping basket on a white background. In the basket, there are fresh vegetables, a loaf of bread, a bottle of milk and two bags of pasta. The colour palette is bright orange and white. Above the basket, orange letters say, "The lowest prices in town." Under the basket, it says, "Full basket: only £15." A button says, "Shop online now." The advert appears on cooking websites.
right1: The superlative "lowest" makes a strong claim that PriceRight beats every other supermarket in town.
right2: Showing a full basket for £15 makes the claim about prices feel real.
right3: The bright orange colour palette makes the advert cheerful and easy to notice.
wrong1: The alliteration in "The lowest prices in town" makes the headline catchy and memorable for readers.
wrong2: Testimonials from happy shoppers under the basket prove that prices really are lowest.
wrong3: The almost empty basket shows how little shoppers can actually buy with £15.

statement: This TV advert for Lumi perfume shows a beautiful young couple walking along an empty beach at sunset. Their white clothes move in the wind, and the light is soft and golden. They look into each other's eyes and laugh, but they never speak. Slow, dreamy music plays, and the waves wash over their feet. At the end, there is a packshot of the glass bottle on the sand, and a soft voice says, "Lumi."
right1: The beautiful couple and soft golden light create an idealised, dreamlike picture of romance.
right2: White clothes and the sunset have connotations of purity, love and freedom for viewers.
right3: Showing no words until "Lumi" makes the brand name feel mysterious and special.
wrong1: The couple's testimonial explains exactly why Lumi is the best perfume for summer.
wrong2: A countdown creates urgency, because the perfume is only sold until the end of summer.
wrong3: Loud, fast music makes the couple's walk feel exciting and full of energy.

statement: This radio advert for the Summer Sound festival begins with a huge crowd cheering and loud rock music. Then an excited voiceover says, "Summer Sound is back!" She lists the famous bands that will play this year, one after another. Then she says, "Tickets on sale Friday at nine. Friday at nine. Don't miss it: Friday at nine!" Last year, all the tickets sold out in two hours. The advert ends with the festival's website.
right1: Repeating "Friday at nine" three times makes the date impossible for listeners to forget.
right2: Mentioning that tickets sold out in two hours last year creates urgency.
right3: The cheering crowd and loud music help listeners imagine being at the festival.
wrong1: The alliteration in "Friday at nine" makes the date sound musical and catchy.
wrong2: A packshot of the festival tickets shows listeners exactly what they will buy.
wrong3: The quiet, calm voiceover makes the festival sound relaxing, peaceful and easy.

statement: This poster for the new Kite phone shows a photo of a quiet city street late at night. The photo is bright and clear, and you can see every star in the sky. In the bottom corner, there is a packshot of the black phone. A small line under the photo says, "Shot on Kite." The tagline says, "See the dark." The poster claims that no other phone takes photos like this in the dark.
right1: The bright night photo itself proves that the camera works well in the dark.
right2: The small line "Shot on Kite" tells readers the photo came from the phone.
right3: Taking clear photos at night is the unique selling point that makes Kite different.
wrong1: The rhetorical question "See the dark" makes readers wonder what the phone can do.
wrong2: The small line "Shot on a professional camera" shows the photo was not taken on a phone.
wrong3: The dark, blurry photo shows how difficult night photography is with any phone.

statement: This TV advert for Sparkle floor cleaner shows a mother mopping a kitchen floor while her children run in with muddy football boots. She smiles and cleans the floor again in a few seconds. A voiceover says, "Nine out of ten mums recommend Sparkle." Then three other women speak to the camera and say how easy it is to use. The last shot is a packshot of the bright purple bottle on the shiny floor.
right1: "Nine out of ten mums" uses a statistic to make the product seem trusted.
right2: Showing only mothers and women cleaning uses a gender stereotype about who does housework.
right3: The three women speaking to the camera act as testimonials for the cleaner.
wrong1: The superlative "Nine out of ten" claims Sparkle is the strongest floor cleaner available today.
wrong2: The voiceover says, "Nine out of ten dads recommend Sparkle," which challenges gender stereotypes.
wrong3: The mother looks angry and tired, so the advert feels realistic and honest.

statement: This online advert for Trendy, a fast fashion shop, shows a row of clothes moving across the screen: jeans, crop tops, jackets and trainers. Each item has a small price under it, from only £5 to £20. Big pink letters say, "New in every day." Under the clothes, a small line says, "Free delivery when you order in the next hour." The advert appears on the social media apps that many teenagers use every day.
right1: "New in every day" makes shoppers feel they must keep checking for new clothes.
right2: Low prices and free delivery within the next hour encourage quick impulse buys.
right3: Appearing on teenagers' social media apps shows the target market is young people.
wrong1: The alliteration in "New in every day" makes the slogan catchy and memorable for teenagers.
wrong2: Testimonials from happy customers under each item prove the clothes are good quality.
wrong3: The high prices suggest the clothes are made to last for many years.

statement: This billboard for FitHouse gym appears in January. It shows a young woman running on a treadmill. She looks strong, fit and happy, and she is not tired. Behind her, there is a large window with a view of the city. The tagline, in big white letters, says, "New year. New you." Under the tagline, the billboard says, "Join this month and pay nothing until February." The gym's logo is a small, bright orange flame.
right1: Appearing in January targets people who have just made their New Year resolutions.
right2: The repetition of "New" in the tagline suggests joining the gym will change your life.
right3: The strong, happy woman is an aspirational image of what you could become.
wrong1: The rhetorical question "New year. New you." makes readers doubt themselves and their bodies.
wrong2: The billboard says new members pay nothing until June, which makes joining feel risk-free.
wrong3: The woman looks exhausted, so the gym seems honest about how hard exercise is.

statement: This poster for Fair Leaf chocolate shows a cocoa farmer called Ama standing in a green field on her farm in Ghana. She is smiling and holding a pile of cocoa beans in her hands. Next to her, there is a quote: "I grew the cocoa in this chocolate." A packshot of the chocolate bar sits at the bottom of the poster. The words "fair", "honest" and "proud" appear on the wrapper in large letters.
right1: Ama's quote works as a testimonial that connects buyers with the real farmer.
right2: Words like "fair" and "honest" have positive connotations that suggest the brand is ethical.
right3: Showing her smiling on her own farm creates an emotional appeal for caring shoppers.
wrong1: The superlative "proud" claims Fair Leaf is the very best chocolate made in Ghana.
wrong2: The small print explains exactly how much Ama is paid for her cocoa.
wrong3: Ama looks unhappy and tired, which makes shoppers feel guilty about buying chocolate.

statement: This social media post for Peak Outdoor shows a woman walking alone on a snowy mountain. She is wearing a grey jacket, a green hat and green boots, and she carries a small backpack. Like every post from this brand, the colours are grey, green and white, and there are no bright colours. The caption says, "Some paths are worth the climb. #GoFurther." The post has no prices and no links to products for sale.
right1: Using the same grey, green and white colours in every post builds a clear brand image.
right2: The woman alone on a mountain makes the brand feel adventurous and aspirational.
right3: Showing no prices makes the post feel like inspiration rather than a normal advert.
wrong1: The superlative "Some paths are worth the climb" says these are the best boots.
wrong2: A discount code in the caption creates urgency for followers to buy now.
wrong3: The bright, colourful clothes make the brand feel loud, young and very exciting.

statement: These screens in a Shanghai metro station show an advert for a shopping app's Double 11 sale. Huge red numbers count down on a gold background: "3 days left!" The same advert appears on every screen along the platform. Each time the train arrives, the advert changes to show a different product: phones, shoes and rice cookers. At the end of each advert, a voice says, "Open the app and add to your basket now!"
right1: The countdown "3 days left!" creates urgency, so shoppers want to act very quickly.
right2: Repeating the advert on every screen along the platform means passengers cannot avoid it.
right3: The voice's imperatives work as a call to action to open the app now.
wrong1: The rhetorical question "Open the app" invites passengers to think about what they need.
wrong2: Testimonials from happy shoppers on the screens make the app seem trustworthy and safe.
wrong3: The advert shows only one product, so passengers remember that product more clearly.

statement: This two-page magazine feature looks like an ordinary article. Its title is "My week without sugar", and it is written in the first person by a busy mother of two from Leeds who describes her tiredness, her cravings and her surprise at how much better she felt. Halfway through, she mentions that she started every morning with a bowl of Pure Oats. The body copy includes facts about fibre and slow-release energy. Only a small grey label in the top corner, reading "Promotion", shows that the brand paid for it.
right1: Because it looks like an ordinary article, the advertorial persuades readers before they realise it is an advert.
right2: Writing in the first person makes the mother's experience feel like an honest personal story.
right3: Facts about fibre and slow-release energy in the body copy add a rational appeal.
wrong1: This is guerrilla marketing, because the brand surprises readers in an unexpected public place.
wrong2: The article is written by a nutrition scientist, which gives the oats an expert, rational appeal.
wrong3: The large, bold "Promotion" label makes it immediately obvious to readers that the brand paid.

statement: On a popular news website, an article titled "Ten best cities for working from home" appears between stories about politics and sport. It has exactly the same font, layout and style of photos as the other articles on the website's front page. Each city is described with beautiful, sunny images of cafés and beaches, and every description ends with the cost of a return flight. At the bottom, a line reads, "In partnership with SkyHop." The airline's logo appears only once, and there is no direct instruction to book anything.
right1: Matching the website's font and layout is native advertising, so the article blends in with real news.
right2: Ending every description with a flight price quietly links each dream city with SkyHop.
right3: There is no direct instruction to book, so this is a soft sell rather than a hard sell.
wrong1: The article is a hard sell, repeatedly telling readers to book a SkyHop flight today.
wrong2: A countdown beside each city creates scarcity, pushing readers to book a flight before seats disappear.
wrong3: The airline's logo appears on every photo, so readers can never forget who is paying.

statement: One Monday morning, people walking through a busy shopping street in Manchester notice giant white footprints painted on the grey pavement. Each print is about a metre long and shows the pattern of a trainer sole. The footprints continue for half a kilometre, around corners and up steps, until they stop outside the door of a new Stride trainer shop. There are no posters and no words, only the footprints and the brand's small logo inside the final print. Within hours, photos of the trail are all over social media.
right1: Painting footprints on the pavement is guerrilla marketing that surprises people in an everyday place.
right2: With no words or posters, curiosity pulls people along the trail to the shop door.
right3: Photos spreading online within hours show viral marketing giving the brand free extra attention.
wrong1: The footprints are targeted advertising, because they only appear to people who searched for trainers.
wrong2: A hashtag printed beside each footprint tells people exactly how to share their photos online.
wrong3: The huge logo on every print makes the brand obvious long before people reach the shop.

statement: This TV advert for Homeguard insurance begins in a dark house at night. A family is asleep upstairs. The camera slowly follows a man's shadow as it moves across the wall of a child's bedroom, while low, tense music builds. A floorboard creaks. Then the screen cuts to black, and a serious voice asks, "If the worst happened, would you be covered?" The strapline appears in white letters: "Homeguard. Sleep soundly." Finally, the voice explains that quotes take five minutes online and that new customers receive a free door alarm.
right1: The shadow in a child's bedroom is a fear appeal that makes parents imagine the worst.
right2: The rhetorical question shifts the fear onto viewers, asking them directly about their own home.
right3: The strapline "Sleep soundly" offers relief after the tension, presenting the insurance as the answer.
wrong1: The free door alarm is a disclaimer that protects Homeguard if something goes wrong.
wrong2: A testimonial from a burglary victim explains how quickly Homeguard paid for her stolen things.
wrong3: Cheerful music and bright lighting make the burglary scene feel like a harmless joke.

statement: On a TV shopping channel, a presenter in a bright red jacket stands behind a shiny kitchen counter, demonstrating the Whirl blender. She speaks quickly and loudly, describing it as "the most incredible machine you will ever own". A counter in the corner of the screen shows how many blenders are left, and the number keeps falling: forty, thirty-two, twenty. Every few seconds she repeats the phone number and urges viewers to call immediately. A banner across the bottom announces that the price will rise by thirty pounds at midnight.
right1: Shouting, repeating the number and urging viewers to call immediately is a classic hard sell.
right2: The falling counter creates scarcity, so viewers fear the blenders will soon be gone.
right3: "The most incredible machine you will ever own" is hyperbole that exaggerates the blender's value.
wrong1: This is a soft sell, because the presenter gently lets viewers decide in their own time.
wrong2: A disclaimer at the bottom warns that the counter does not show the real stock level.
wrong3: The price falls by thirty pounds at midnight, so viewers are encouraged to wait.

statement: This full-page magazine advert for the Volta electric car contains only a small photo of the car in the top left corner. The rest of the page is body copy and tables. The text explains that the car can travel 520 kilometres on one charge, that it costs about two pence per kilometre to run, and that it has received the highest safety rating. A bar chart compares its running costs with those of a similar petrol car. Under the photo, a short caption reads, "The numbers speak for themselves."
right1: Figures on range, cost and safety create a rational appeal based on facts, not feelings.
right2: Making the photo small puts the focus on the body copy and the evidence.
right3: The bar chart lets readers compare costs quickly, which supports the car's claim to save money.
wrong1: The caption "The numbers speak for themselves" is a neologism that the brand has invented.
wrong2: The bar chart compares Volta with other electric cars, showing it is the cheapest of its kind.
wrong3: The huge, beautiful photo of the car leaves little space for any technical information.

statement: After a university student searches online for cheap camping trips in Scotland, she begins to see adverts for Ridgeline tents on almost every website she visits. The adverts show young people laughing around a campfire under the stars, with mountains and a lake behind them. The text says, "You've been thinking about it. Now go." One advert even mentions the area she searched for. The tents are light and inexpensive, and the adverts appear mainly late in the evening, when she is most likely to be browsing on her phone.
right1: Showing tent adverts after her search is targeted advertising based on her online behaviour.
right2: Mentioning the area she searched for makes the advert feel personal, almost like it knows her.
right3: "You've been thinking about it. Now go." uses direct address and an imperative to push her.
wrong1: Appearing on almost every website she visits is guerrilla marketing in an unexpected public place.
wrong2: A disclaimer explains to her that the adverts are chosen using her search history.
wrong3: The adverts appear early in the morning, when she is busy and unlikely to be browsing.

statement: This TV advert for Clearwell still water shows a woman doing yoga on the edge of a cliff at sunrise. The sea is calm below her, and the only sounds are waves and birds. She moves slowly and breathes deeply. A tall glass bottle of Clearwell stands beside her mat, catching the light, but she never opens it or drinks from it. There is no voiceover. At the very end, a few words appear in a thin, white font: "Clearwell. Find your stillness." The brand donates to ocean protection charities.
right1: The bottle is never opened, so the advert sells a calm lifestyle rather than the water itself.
right2: With no voiceover or prices, the advert uses a soft sell that feels peaceful, not pushy.
right3: Donating to ocean charities supports brand values connected to nature, calm and the sea.
wrong1: Her yoga routine is a rational appeal, giving viewers practical reasons to choose Clearwell water.
wrong2: A voiceover lists the minerals in the water, giving viewers clear facts about its health benefits.
wrong3: Loud music and fast editing make the yoga on the cliff look energetic and competitive.

statement: This billboard for Crunchers crisps shows a man in a smart suit who has just dropped an entire bag of crisps on the floor of a busy, open-plan office during a meeting. His colleagues are staring at him, and his face is frozen in horror. Crisps are scattered everywhere. Above the scene, huge orange letters announce: "Avoid a snackcident." Underneath, in smaller letters, the billboard adds, "Crunchers. Now in a resealable bag." A packshot of the new bag, with its zip at the top, appears in the bottom right corner.
right1: "Snackcident" is a neologism that mixes "snack" and "accident" to make the strapline funny and memorable.
right2: The embarrassing scene in the office shows exactly the problem the resealable bag is meant to solve.
right3: The packshot shows the zip clearly, so readers can see the new feature for themselves.
wrong1: The man's horror is a fear appeal, using shock tactics to warn people about eating at work.
wrong2: A disclaimer warns that the bag only reseals properly if the zip is closed completely.
wrong3: The calm, tidy office scene suggests that eating crisps at work is never a problem.

statement: This government poster against drink-driving shows a car that has crashed into a tree on a dark, wet country road. The front of the car is completely crushed, and broken glass covers the road. The photo is lit by the blue lights of an emergency vehicle. On the back seat, we can see a small pink child's shoe. There are no people anywhere in the picture. The strapline, in plain white letters, says, "One more drink isn't worth it." The poster appears in pubs, bars and petrol stations in December.
right1: The crushed car and broken glass use shock tactics to make the danger feel real.
right2: The child's shoe makes viewers imagine a victim without showing one, which is more disturbing.
right3: Displaying it in pubs in December reaches drinkers at the time and place it matters most.
wrong1: The strapline "One more drink isn't worth it" is hyperbole that exaggerates a small risk.
wrong2: A testimonial from a police officer describes the crash and what happened to the family.
wrong3: Bright daylight and a clean road make the scene look calm, peaceful and almost safe.

statement: This magazine advert for Serene foundation shows a close-up of a model's face. Her skin is completely smooth and even, without a single line, pore or freckle, and it seems to glow. Her eyes look directly at the reader, and her lips are slightly open. The headline claims, "Flawless skin in one step." Beside the bottle, a list of ingredients is described as "advanced". At the very bottom of the page, in tiny grey print that is difficult to read, a line says, "Image digitally enhanced. Model wears additional products."
right1: Skin without a single pore suggests airbrushing, creating a beauty standard no real person can match.
right2: The disclaimer is in tiny grey print, so most readers will probably never notice it.
right3: Calling the ingredients "advanced" gives the product a scientific feel without actually explaining anything specific.
wrong1: The disclaimer at the bottom works as anchorage, telling readers to buy the foundation today.
wrong2: A brand ambassador's quote explains that she has worn Serene foundation every day for years.
wrong3: The large, bold disclaimer makes it obvious to every reader that the photo has been changed.

statement: In this TV advert for Bloom skincare, a well-known actress sits in a bright, simple bathroom in the early morning. At first, she is wearing no make-up, and her hair is tied back simply. Speaking softly, almost in a whisper, she tells the viewer about her morning routine as she gently applies the cream. She does not mention price or offers. Instead, she says, "I've trusted Bloom for ten years." At the end, the brand name appears, followed by the words "Bloom ambassador since 2016". Calm piano music plays throughout.
right1: As a brand ambassador, the actress links Bloom with her fame and her long career.
right2: Speaking softly in a simple bathroom creates an intimate mode of address, like a friend talking.
right3: Avoiding prices and offers makes this a soft sell based on trust rather than pressure.
wrong1: The actress is an influencer whose sponsored post includes a discount code for her followers.
wrong2: A disclaimer at the end reminds viewers that the actress wore extra make-up during filming.
wrong3: Her loud, fast way of speaking makes the advert feel like a hard sell.

statement: This poster announces a new look for Bun & Go, a burger chain that has existed since the 1990s. The old red and yellow logo has been replaced with a simple dark green circle and the brand name in lowercase white letters. The photo shows a single burger on plain brown paper, surrounded by fresh green lettuce, tomatoes and herbs. The strapline says, "Fresh is back." Underneath, the body copy explains that the chain now uses local beef and paper packaging. The menu, however, has hardly changed since last year.
right1: The new green logo and lowercase letters are a rebrand towards a fresher, more natural identity.
right2: Plain brown paper and fresh herbs give the burger connotations of simplicity, freshness and care.
right3: The unchanged menu suggests the rebrand may change the image more than the food.
wrong1: The strapline "Fresh is back" is a neologism, a new word made for the campaign.
wrong2: A focus group's opinions appear on the poster to prove that customers prefer the new look.
wrong3: Keeping the old red and yellow logo shows the brand is proud of its long history.

statement: This advert appears in a small magazine for people who collect fountain pens. It shows a single photograph of a dark blue fountain pen lying on a sheet of handwritten paper. Below the photo, a long paragraph explains how each Inkwell pen is made by hand in a workshop in Edinburgh, how long it takes to shape the gold nib, and which wood is used for the case. The language is calm, careful and detailed. The price, £480, is given clearly at the end, along with the workshop's postal address.
right1: Advertising in a magazine for pen collectors targets a small, niche market of enthusiasts.
right2: The detailed body copy about craft gives readers rational reasons to pay a high price.
right3: Calm, careful language matches the slow, handmade process and suits the patience of serious collectors.
wrong1: Placing the advert in a specialist magazine is mass marketing aimed at as many people as possible.
wrong2: Scarcity is created by saying that only fifty pens will ever be made this year.
wrong3: Hiding the price suggests the pen is so exclusive that readers should not ask.

statement: This TV advert for ValueMart supermarket shows dozens of different shoppers filling their trolleys to a cheerful, catchy song. There is a student buying pasta, an elderly couple choosing fruit, a young dad with twins, and a group of teenagers buying snacks for a party. Everyone is smiling; nobody looks stressed. The camera moves quickly from one person to the next. Price labels pop up beside the products. The strapline appears at the end: "ValueMart. Good food for everyone." The advert is shown at peak times on the main channels.
right1: Showing shoppers of every age and type positions ValueMart as a supermarket for the mass market.
right2: The strapline "Good food for everyone" supports the idea that nobody is left out.
right3: Showing the advert at peak times on the main channels reaches the widest possible audience.
wrong1: The advert targets a niche market of wealthy shoppers who want rare, expensive food.
wrong2: A disclaimer explains that the prices shown are only available in larger ValueMart stores.
wrong3: Quiet, slow music and stressed faces make shopping at ValueMart seem like a difficult chore.

statement: This short online video shows a puppy chasing a Robo robot vacuum cleaner around a living room. Every time the puppy gets close, the robot turns away, and the puppy falls over its own feet. It looks like home footage filmed on a phone. There is no voiceover and no music, just the sound of the puppy barking and someone laughing. The brand name appears only once, on top of the robot. The video has been shared millions of times, and many viewers did not realise it was an advert.
right1: The funny, shareable puppy clip is viral marketing that spreads the brand without paid adverts.
right2: Home footage on a phone makes the video feel real rather than like a polished advert.
right3: Showing the brand only once is a soft sell, so viewers enjoy it without feeling pushed.
wrong1: The video is an advertorial, an article written to look like ordinary news about vacuums.
wrong2: A voiceover explains the robot's features while the puppy chases it around the room.
wrong3: The brand name appears constantly, so every viewer knows immediately that it is an advert.

statement: This poster for the Living Forest charity shows a large photo of an empty brown field under a grey sky. There are a few tree stumps and some deep tyre tracks in the mud, and nothing else. Without words, the image could be any field in the countryside. However, a single caption at the bottom changes its meaning: "This was a forest last year." Under the caption, a smaller line asks readers to sponsor a tree for £5. The poster is printed on recycled paper and displayed in railway stations.
right1: The caption is anchorage: it fixes the photo's meaning, turning an ordinary field into a loss.
right2: The empty field and stumps use shock tactics once readers understand what has disappeared.
right3: Printing on recycled paper matches the charity's values and makes its message more believable.
wrong1: The strapline uses a neologism to describe the forest in a new and memorable way.
wrong2: A countdown on the poster shows how many trees are cut down every second, creating urgency.
wrong3: The bright, colourful photo of a healthy forest makes the problem look already solved.

statement: During one week, twenty small influencers, each with between five and fifty thousand followers, post photos using Kiwi hair oil. They are not famous, and their posts look like ordinary moments from their lives: a morning routine, a gym bag, a messy bathroom shelf. Every post includes the same discount code, KIWI15, and most speak to followers in a casual, friendly way, such as "OK guys, you have to try this." Some posts include "#ad" at the end of the caption, but several do not mention a partnership at all.
right1: Using many small influencers is a form of influencer marketing that feels more personal than one celebrity.
right2: The casual mode of address, "OK guys", makes the posts sound like advice from friends.
right3: Posts without "#ad" raise questions about regulation, because followers may not realise they are adverts.
wrong1: The posts are native advertising, because they appear inside the articles of a news website.
wrong2: Every influencer uses a different discount code, so the whole campaign feels personal and unplanned.
wrong3: Every post is clearly labelled "#ad", so followers always know they are being sold to.

statement: This radio advert for the LuckySpin betting app begins with the sound of a crowd cheering at a football match. An excited voiceover shouts that new customers who sign up today can receive £50 in free bets. He repeats the offer twice and tells listeners to download the app right now before the weekend's matches. Then, in the last few seconds, a different voice reads a long legal disclaimer extremely quickly: "Over eighteens only. Terms apply. When the fun stops, stop." The disclaimer is almost impossible for listeners to understand.
right1: The fast disclaimer meets regulation on paper but is almost impossible for listeners to understand.
right2: The cheering crowd links betting with the excitement and energy of watching live football.
right3: Repeating the offer and saying "right now" is a hard sell that pushes listeners to act.
wrong1: The disclaimer is a strapline that sums up the brand's identity in one memorable line.
wrong2: The voiceover offers £5 in free bets, which sounds too small to be persuasive.
wrong3: The disclaimer is read slowly and clearly, so every listener fully understands the risks involved.

statement: This TV advert for Fairway Bank shows a young couple sitting at a kitchen table with a laptop, looking at their savings. A calm, clear voiceover explains the bank's new account: an interest rate of 4.5%, no monthly fees, and money that can be withdrawn at any time. Simple graphics show the numbers growing over five years. The couple are relaxed, and the kitchen is tidy and quiet. At the end, the strapline appears: "Fairway. Plan for tomorrow." There is no music, only the voice and some soft background sounds.
right1: Giving the interest rate and no fees creates a rational appeal based on clear facts.
right2: Graphics of savings growing over five years help viewers picture their own future money.
right3: The calm voice and quiet kitchen suggest the bank is safe, sensible and trustworthy.
wrong1: The calm voiceover uses a fear appeal, warning viewers what will happen without savings.
wrong2: Scarcity is created because the account is only open to the first thousand customers.
wrong3: Loud music and fast editing make the savings account feel exciting rather than safe and sensible.

statement: This poster for Volley sportswear shows a female sprinter at the start of a race. She has a running blade in place of her lower left leg, and she is staring down the long, empty track with total focus. The whole photo is in black and white, apart from her orange Volley vest. The strapline, in large white capitals, says, "No limits." There is no other text and no product information. The poster appears around stadiums during a major international athletics event, and the athlete is a famous Paralympic champion.
right1: Choosing a Paralympic champion shows the brand's values of determination, strength and inclusion for all athletes.
right2: The orange vest is the only colour, so the eye goes straight to the brand.
