right3: The strapline "No limits" is hyperbole that also works as a message about the athlete.
wrong1: The strapline is anchorage that explains in detail what the sportswear is made from.
wrong2: Body copy beside the photo lists the vest's features, price and the shops that sell it.
wrong3: The bright, full-colour photo makes the orange vest blend into the busy stadium behind her.

statement: This online advert for Kicks Club shows a pair of white and gold trainers on a dark background, lit from below so that they glow. Only the outline of the brand's logo is visible. Big text says, "Members only. 100 pairs." Underneath, a countdown shows that the trainers will be released on Saturday at ten in the morning, and that only registered members can buy them. To become a member, customers must pay a yearly fee of £50. The advert appears on websites and forums read by serious trainer collectors.
right1: The words "Members only. 100 pairs." create scarcity, making the trainers feel rare and desirable.
right2: Advertising on collectors' forums targets a niche market that cares deeply about rare, limited releases.
right3: The yearly fee makes buying feel exclusive, as if customers must earn the right.
wrong1: The countdown is a fear appeal that warns collectors about the dangers of fake trainers.
wrong2: The trainers are released on a weekday evening, when collectors are most likely to be free.
wrong3: The trainers are available to everyone in every shop, so collectors can relax and wait.

statement: In this TV advert for Bright toothpaste, a man in a white coat stands in a clean, modern laboratory. He holds up a large model of a tooth and explains, using a diagram, how the toothpaste's formula protects enamel from acid. Graphs and percentages appear on the screen beside him. He speaks seriously and clearly, like a teacher in a class. In very small text at the bottom of the screen, for less than two seconds, a line says, "Actor portrayal." The advert ends with the claim, "Recommended by dentists."
right1: The white coat and laboratory suggest expertise, even though the man is only an actor.
right2: The diagram, graphs and percentages create a rational appeal that makes the toothpaste seem scientific.
right3: Showing "Actor portrayal" for under two seconds suggests the advert may be trying to manipulate viewers.
wrong1: The man is a brand ambassador, a famous dentist who has used Bright for many years.
wrong2: A focus group of real patients explains how their teeth improved after using Bright.
wrong3: The disclaimer stays on screen throughout, so viewers clearly know the man is not a dentist.

statement: In this online video, a popular travel vlogger spends five days exploring the Greek island of Lefkada. She swims in clear blue bays, eats in small family restaurants and talks warmly about the friendly local people. The video is beautiful and relaxed, and she never asks viewers to buy anything. At the very beginning, she says quickly, "This trip was paid for by Visit Lefkada," and a small label in the corner says "Paid partnership". Many comments under the video say that they now want to visit the island too.
right1: This is sponsored content: the tourism board paid, but the video feels like a personal holiday.
right2: Never asking viewers to buy anything makes it a soft sell built on enjoyment and trust.
right3: Saying "paid for" quickly at the start meets regulation without spoiling the relaxed mood.
wrong1: The video is a hard sell, because the vlogger repeatedly urges viewers to book immediately.
wrong2: Scarcity is created by a discount code that only works for the first fifty viewers.
wrong3: The vlogger hides the payment completely, so viewers never learn that she was sponsored.

statement: This magazine advert for the Barista coffee machine shows a large, bright loft apartment with high windows and white walls. A man in his thirties, wearing a casual shirt, stands by the window holding a coffee cup and looking out at the city. Everything in the room is neat and expensive: a leather sofa, a record player, a shelf of design books. The silver coffee machine sits on a white marble counter near the window. The only text is "Barista. Your mornings, perfected." The advert appears in a design magazine.
right1: The expensive loft sells a lifestyle, suggesting the machine belongs in a stylish, successful life.
right2: Placing the advert in a design magazine targets readers who care about how things look.
right3: The short strapline "Your mornings, perfected" promises a better daily routine, not just better coffee.
wrong1: The advert uses a rational appeal, listing the machine's technical features and price for readers.
wrong2: The man in the loft is in his sixties, so the audience positioning targets retired readers.
wrong3: The messy, crowded family flat makes the machine look practical for busy everyday life.

statement: This billboard for Cloud office chairs shows a businessman asleep in a grey leather office chair that is floating high above a city. Soft white clouds surround him, and a few birds fly past his feet. He looks completely relaxed, with his tie loose and a smile on his face. The strapline, in big blue letters, says, "The most comfortable chair in the universe." Under it, smaller letters say, "Sit back. You've earned it." The billboard is placed on a busy road leading into the financial district of the city.
right1: "The most comfortable chair in the universe" is hyperbole that nobody could actually check.
right2: The floating chair and clouds turn the idea of comfort into a dreamlike image.
right3: Placing the billboard near the financial district targets tired office workers on their way in.
wrong1: The clouds are anchorage, fixing the meaning of the strapline as a weather forecast.
wrong2: Body copy explains the chair's features and how it supports the back during long days.
wrong3: The businessman sits stiffly and looks stressed, so the chair seems hard and uncomfortable.

statement: For one week in July, a metro station in central Shanghai is transformed into a beach by Sun Travel. Real sand covers part of the platform, and deckchairs and colourful beach umbrellas stand along the walls. The sound of waves and seagulls plays from hidden speakers. Tired commuters in suits take photos and lie in the deckchairs while they wait for trains. Small signs say, "Your holiday is closer than you think," with a code for a discount. Videos of the station have been shared widely on Chinese social media.
right1: Turning a metro station into a beach is guerrilla marketing that surprises commuters on their way to work.
right2: The real sand and sound of waves let tired commuters experience a holiday feeling directly.
right3: People sharing videos online is viral marketing that spreads the campaign far beyond the station.
wrong1: The beach is native advertising, because it matches the style of the other articles in a magazine.
wrong2: A disclaimer on the signs explains that the discount is only valid for flights to Thailand.
wrong3: Commuters ignore the beach and walk past quickly, so the campaign attracts almost no attention.

statement: This TV advert for Shield antivirus software begins in a dark room where a hacker sits before several screens. His face is lit blue by the monitors, and we cannot see his eyes. Fast, nervous electronic music plays in the background. On one screen, we see a family's photos, bank details and passwords appearing one by one. A loud voice says, "Every 39 seconds, someone is hacked. Will you be next?" The strapline appears: "Shield. Don't wait until it's too late." The special offer for new customers ends on Sunday.
right1: The hacker's hidden face and tense music create a fear appeal about online danger.
right2: Showing a family's photos, bank details and passwords makes the threat feel personal to viewers.
right3: The strapline "Don't wait until it's too late" adds urgency to the fear already created.
wrong1: The rhetorical question is anchorage that explains exactly how the software protects family computers.
wrong2: A focus group of parents explains why they chose Shield for their children's laptops.
wrong3: Bright, cheerful music makes hacking seem like a harmless game rather than a real threat.

statement: This new, limited edition bag of Crunchers crisps has a large badge on the front that says, "You chose this flavour!" Last summer, the brand asked the public to vote online between three new flavours, and more than a million people took part in just two weeks. The winning flavour, chilli and lime, is shown in a packshot with a bright green and red background. On the back, the body copy thanks fans for voting and invites them to suggest next year's flavour on the brand's website or social media.
right1: Letting the public choose the flavour makes customers feel involved, which builds brand loyalty.
right2: "You chose this flavour!" uses direct address, so buyers feel the crisps belong partly to them.
right3: Mentioning over a million voters suggests the flavour is popular, which creates a bandwagon effect.
wrong1: The public vote is a focus group, a small private group paid to test flavours in secret.
wrong2: The winning flavour, cheese and onion, shows the public prefers safe and traditional choices over new ones.
wrong3: The brand chose the flavour without asking anyone, so the badge sounds honest and modest.

statement: This bar of Root & Branch soap is wrapped in plain brown paper and tied with natural string. There is no plastic anywhere on the packaging. A small paper label shows a simple hand-drawn tree. On the back, a short paragraph explains the brand's values: every ingredient is grown on small farms, nothing is tested on animals, and ten per cent of profits support forest projects. The language is simple and personal, ending with the words, "Thank you for choosing gently." The bar costs £7, much more than ordinary soap.
right1: The brown paper and string reflect brand values of simplicity and care for the planet.
right2: The body copy states the brand's values clearly, giving shoppers ethical reasons to pay more.
right3: The personal language, "Thank you for choosing gently," makes buyers feel good about their choice.
wrong1: The hand-drawn tree is a neologism, a new word the brand has invented for its packaging.
wrong2: The body copy says half the profits support forests, making the price seem fair.
wrong3: Shiny plastic packaging contradicts the brand's environmental values and makes the soap look cheap and ordinary.

statement: This TV advert for the Regent saloon car shows a grey-haired man in his sixties driving slowly along a coastal road at sunset. Gentle piano music plays. He is alone in the car, relaxed and smiling slightly, with one hand on the wheel. The car's interior is shown in close-up: soft leather seats, wooden panels and a quiet engine. There is no talk of speed or price. At the end, a calm male voice says, "The Regent. You've arrived." The advert is shown during evening news programmes and golf tournaments.
right1: The grey-haired driver and golf tournaments show the audience positioning towards older, wealthy men.
right2: Close-ups of leather, wood and a quiet engine suggest comfort and quality rather than speed.
right3: The strapline "You've arrived" suggests success, as if buying the car shows you have made it.
wrong1: The advert is a hard sell, using fast speech and urgent offers to push older viewers.
wrong2: Body copy lists the car's price, fuel use and safety rating for careful buyers.
wrong3: Loud rock music and a fast, noisy drive make the car seem young and wild.

statement: This magazine advert for the Wave mobile network is aimed at teenagers. It shows three friends taking a selfie together on a city rooftop at night, all laughing. The text is written as if it were a text message between friends: "No cap, Wave is lowkey the best deal rn." Below this, the body copy uses invented words such as "datastic" and "unlimitless" to describe the new unlimited phone plan. The price, £12 a month, is printed in a speech bubble, along with the line, "Ur parents will approve too."
right1: The casual mode of address copies teenagers' text messages, so the brand sounds like a friend.
right2: Neologisms such as "datastic" and "unlimitless" make the advert playful and memorable for young readers.
right3: "Ur parents will approve too" reassures teenagers that the price will not cause arguments at home.
wrong1: The speech bubble is a disclaimer that hides the real price in tiny legal text.
wrong2: The price, £42 a month, is printed in a speech bubble, which seems too expensive for teenagers.
wrong3: The formal, polite language makes the advert sound like a letter from a bank manager.

statement: This poster for the Quit Now campaign shows a single cigarette on a black background. However, the cigarette looks like the fuse of a bomb: the end is burning with bright orange sparks, and a thin line of smoke rises above it. There are no people or other objects in the image. Below the picture, white letters say, "Every cigarette brings it closer." Underneath, in smaller letters, there is the number of a free, confidential helpline. The posters appear on the sides of city buses and in hospital waiting rooms.
right1: Showing the cigarette as a bomb fuse is a fear appeal that links smoking with disaster.
right2: "Every cigarette brings it closer" leaves readers to imagine what "it" is, which is more disturbing.
right3: Placing posters in hospital waiting rooms reaches smokers when health is already on their minds.
wrong1: The strapline is a neologism that combines "cigarette" and "bomb" into one new and memorable word.
wrong2: A testimonial from a former smoker explains how the helpline helped him to quit.
wrong3: The bright, friendly colours and smiling people make quitting seem fun, light and easy.

statement: When a customer visits the website of Trendy, an online clothes shop, a bright pop-up appears immediately with a red countdown timer: "Offer ends in 09:59." The pop-up promises 40% off absolutely everything if the customer orders before the timer reaches zero. The numbers tick down second by second, and a message underneath says, "23 people are looking at this item right now." However, if the customer reloads the page, the timer starts again from ten minutes. Several consumer groups have already complained about the website to the advertising regulator.
right1: The countdown timer creates false scarcity, because it restarts every time the page reloads.
right2: "23 people are looking" creates a bandwagon effect, suggesting that other shoppers might buy the item first.
right3: Complaints to the advertising regulator suggest the website may be manipulating its customers in an unfair way.
wrong1: The pop-up is a soft sell that gently lets customers decide in their own time.
wrong2: A disclaimer under the timer explains honestly that the offer will return again tomorrow morning.
wrong3: The timer always stays at ten minutes, so customers feel no pressure to hurry.

statement: This page in a weekend newspaper looks like a normal health article. Its headline asks, "Are you getting enough vitamins this winter?" The article interviews a nutrition expert and describes how tiredness, low mood and colds are common in the dark winter months. Near the end, it recommends Vita gummies, describing them as "the easy way to stay healthy". A photo shows the colourful, fruit-shaped sweets in a glass bowl. At the bottom, small text says "Advertisement feature", and a line warns that supplements should not replace a varied diet.
right1: Presenting the advert as a health article is an advertorial that borrows the newspaper's trusted voice.
right2: Interviewing a nutrition expert gives the recommendation authority before the product is even named.
right3: The warning about a varied diet is a disclaimer that may be easy to miss.
wrong1: The article is guerrilla marketing, because it appears suddenly in an unexpected public street.
wrong2: The article names the gummies in its first line, so readers know at once it is an advert.
wrong3: The large "Advertisement feature" title at the top makes the advert obvious from the start.

statement: This two-minute TV advert for Lumi perfume is like a short film. A young woman runs through the streets of Paris at night, past glowing cafés and shop windows, across a bridge and up the stairs of an old building. She opens a door onto a rooftop full of light and music, where a group of friends welcome her. Nobody speaks, and we never learn her story. The perfume bottle is not shown until the final three seconds, when it appears on a black screen with the single word "Lumi".
right1: With no words until the end, the advert relies on mood and mystery rather than facts.
right2: The glowing Paris streets and rooftop party sell an exciting lifestyle, not the perfume's smell.
right3: Hiding the bottle until the last seconds makes the brand name the final, memorable reveal.
wrong1: The advert uses a rational appeal, explaining the perfume's ingredients and price in detail.
wrong2: A voiceover tells the woman's story, explaining why she is running through Paris at night.
wrong3: The bottle appears in every scene, so viewers always know exactly what is being sold.

statement: This billboard for Sterling Cars is bright red and covered in large yellow letters. The main headline shouts, "0% finance! Today only!" Below it, three new cars are shown with huge prices beside them, and a starburst shape says, "Huge savings!" A huge arrow points down the road towards the garage, which is only two hundred metres away. At the bottom, in very small white text, a disclaimer explains that the offer depends on a large first payment and is only available to some customers with a good credit history.
right1: Shouting headlines, "Today only!" and huge prices beside the cars make this a classic hard sell.
right2: The arrow pointing two hundred metres away encourages passing drivers to turn in and act immediately.
right3: The tiny disclaimer shows the "0% finance" offer is far less simple than it looks.
wrong1: The starburst "Huge savings!" is anchorage that explains the exact terms of the finance offer.
wrong2: The arrow points to a garage twenty kilometres away, so drivers must plan a long trip.
wrong3: Soft colours and calm language make this a gentle soft sell for careful buyers.

statement: After a young man orders fast food from a delivery app late at night several times in one week, he begins to see adverts for the FitHouse gym on his phone. One shows a fit man of his age running at dawn and says, "Tired of feeling tired?" Another shows a pair of jeans that no longer fit around the waist, with the line, "It's not too late to start." The adverts appear mostly after midnight. Each one offers a free first week and a button that says "Start tomorrow".
right1: The gym adverts are targeted using his food orders, so they seem to know his habits.
right2: "Tired of feeling tired?" is a rhetorical question that touches on his private worries about his health.
right3: The jeans that no longer fit create a fear appeal about his changing body.
wrong1: The adverts are guerrilla marketing, painted on the pavements where he walks home every night.
wrong2: The adverts offer a free first month, which makes the gym feel generous and low-risk.
wrong3: The adverts appear during the day, when he is busy at work and least likely to look.

statement: This magazine advert for Aurum watches shows a famous international footballer in a dark suit, sitting alone in an empty stadium at night, under the floodlights. He is looking down at the gold watch on his wrist and smiling slightly to himself. Under the photo, a paragraph of body copy describes his career: how he started playing on the streets of Lagos and became the captain of his national team. It ends with the line, "Every great moment is timed. Aurum." There is no price, only the brand's website address.
right1: As a brand ambassador, the footballer links Aurum with success, leadership and great moments.
right2: The body copy's story from Lagos streets to captain makes the watch part of an inspiring journey.
right3: The empty stadium and floodlights make him look like a hero in a quiet, personal moment.
wrong1: The footballer's career story is hyperbole, because it is obviously invented and completely impossible to believe.
wrong2: Scarcity is created by saying only fifty watches with his signature will ever be made.
wrong3: The crowded, noisy stadium makes the footballer look like just one face among many.

statement: This poster introduces the new look of Fairway Bank, which has been a traditional, serious bank for over a hundred years. The old dark blue shield has gone. In its place, the name "fairway" is written in round, lowercase letters, and the "y" curves upwards like a smile. The background is bright yellow, and the logo looks almost like a cartoon. The new strapline says, "Banking that's on your side." Underneath, the body copy explains that the bank's app has been redesigned to be simpler and friendlier for young customers.
right1: Replacing the serious shield with round lowercase letters is a rebrand towards a friendlier identity.
right2: The "y" shaped like a smile gives the logo a warm and cheerful connotation for customers.
right3: The new strapline suggests the bank wants young customers to see it as an ally.
wrong1: The bright yellow background is a disclaimer that protects the bank from legal problems.
wrong2: A focus group of students explains on the poster why they prefer the new design.
wrong3: Keeping the dark blue shield shows the bank wants to look even more serious and traditional.

statement: This Christmas TV advert for Hollins supermarket shows many different families preparing one meal in their own homes: a grandmother teaching her grandson to roast potatoes, two dads decorating a table, a student cooking for friends in a tiny flat, and a large Indian family making dessert. Warm, gentle music plays, and the camera moves smoothly from kitchen to kitchen. At the end, the screen splits, and all the families appear around their tables at the same time. The strapline appears in gold letters: "However you celebrate, Hollins is there."
right1: Showing many kinds of families positions Hollins as a supermarket for the whole mass market.
right2: Including two dads, a student and an Indian family shows the brand's inclusive values.
right3: The split screen joins every family together, supporting the strapline's message about Hollins being there.
wrong1: The advert targets a niche market of wealthy families who want expensive, rare foods.
wrong2: Price labels pop up beside each dish, giving viewers a rational reason to shop there.
wrong3: Only one kind of family is shown, so the advert seems narrow and old-fashioned.

statement: In a popular car racing video game, players drive through a city at night at very high speed, avoiding traffic and the police. Along the road, there are huge, bright digital billboards for Volt cola, showing the red can and the brand's logo. When players pass a certain point, a Volt cola truck drives across the road. The billboards fit naturally into the game's world, and many players hardly notice them. The game is mainly played by teenagers and young adults, and it is completely free to download on phones.
right1: The billboards inside the game are native advertising, because they fit naturally into its world.
right2: Players hardly notice the adverts, so the brand reaches them without seeming to sell.
right3: Placing the cola in a free game targets teenagers and young adults where they spend time.
wrong1: The billboards are a hard sell, shouting prices and offers at players during every race.
wrong2: A disclaimer at the start of each race tells players that Volt cola paid for the billboards.
wrong3: The billboards look completely different from the game, so players notice them immediately and find them annoying.

statement: This magazine advert for MaxBuild protein powder shows a man with no shirt standing in a gym. His muscles are huge and perfectly defined, and his skin is smooth and shining under strong lights. The headline says, "Gains guaranteed. Results in 30 days." A large black tub of powder stands on a bench beside him, with gold letters on the label. Next to a star at the bottom of the page, small print explains that results depend on exercise and diet. Experts say the photo has clearly been digitally changed.
right1: The perfectly defined muscles and smooth skin suggest airbrushing, creating an ideal that no real body could achieve.
right2: "Gains guaranteed" makes a confident promise that the small print at the bottom then quietly weakens.
right3: The disclaimer about exercise and diet shows the powder alone may not give these results.
wrong1: The headline is anchorage that explains in detail how the protein powder works in the body.
wrong2: The headline promises results in three days, which is hyperbole that few readers would believe.
wrong3: The man's ordinary, untouched body makes the results feel realistic and achievable for anyone.

statement: This radio advert for EaseAll pain tablets begins with a tired woman sighing loudly, then describing a terrible headache that stopped her from working. A calm male voice explains that EaseAll contains ibuprofen and starts working in just fifteen minutes. He gives a few simple facts: suitable for adults, available in all chemists and supermarkets, and gentle on the stomach. At the end, he says clearly, "Always read the label. If symptoms continue, speak to your pharmacist." The final words are spoken slowly, so that every listener can hear them.
right1: "Always read the label" is spoken slowly, showing the advert follows medicine regulation carefully.
right2: Simple facts about ibuprofen and fifteen minutes create a rational appeal for headache sufferers.
right3: The woman's sigh and description of pain help listeners recognise their own headaches immediately.
wrong1: The final warning is hyperbole that exaggerates the dangers of taking ordinary pain tablets.
wrong2: The voice says EaseAll starts working in fifty minutes, which makes it sound slow.
wrong3: The warning is read very fast, so listeners can hardly understand the safety advice.

statement: This TV advert for Crunchtastic cereal shows a family of colourful cartoon animals dancing around a kitchen table. A loud, catchy song plays, and the word "Crunchtastic" is sung again and again by different characters: the dog, the cat and even the talking toaster. Each time the word is sung, it appears in bright yellow letters on the screen. Then real children and parents are shown eating the cereal together at a sunny table and laughing. The advert is shown at breakfast time and during family programmes in the evening.
right1: "Crunchtastic" is a neologism that combines "crunch" and "fantastic" to make the cereal's name fun.
right2: Repeating the word again and again makes the name stick firmly in children's memories.
right3: Showing it at breakfast and during family programmes targets the mass market of parents and children.
wrong1: The cartoon animals are brand ambassadors, famous real celebrities paid to represent the cereal for years.
wrong2: Body copy lists the vitamins and fibre in the cereal on screen for health-conscious parents.
wrong3: A quiet, slow song makes breakfast feel calm, so the brand name is easily forgotten.

statement: This poster for Bright Energy shows a large, simple bar chart on a white background. The bars show a typical family's electricity bill falling year by year after switching to solar panels: from £1,200 to £400. The chart is in calm shades of green and blue. Under the chart, the caption says, "This is what switching looks like." A short paragraph explains that the panels are installed in one day and come with a twenty-year guarantee. The brand's values, "clean, simple, fair", appear in small letters next to the logo.
right1: The bar chart creates a rational appeal, showing savings with clear numbers instead of emotion.
right2: The caption works as anchorage, telling readers that the chart shows life after switching to Bright.
right3: Calm greens and blues support the brand values of being clean, simple and fair.
wrong1: The chart is hyperbole, because it shows the family's bills falling to zero overnight.
wrong2: A testimonial from a happy family explains how much money they saved last year.
wrong3: Dramatic red and black colours create a fear appeal about rising electricity bills next winter.

statement: In a livestream on a Chinese shopping app, a popular host sits in a bright pink studio surrounded by boxes of face masks. She speaks extremely quickly, holding up the product and applying one to her own face. Every few minutes she shouts, "Only five thousand left! Three, two, one, link's live!" The number of buyers flashes on the screen, rising rapidly. Comments from viewers scroll past quickly, many asking about prices and skin types. The host calls viewers "family" and promises a free gift to the first thousand customers.
right1: Shouting "Only five thousand left!" and counting down is a hard sell that rushes buyers.
right2: The rising number of buyers creates a bandwagon effect, so viewers want to join in.
right3: Calling viewers "family" is a warm mode of address that builds trust and closeness.
wrong1: The livestream is an advertorial, written to look like an ordinary article in a newspaper.
wrong2: A disclaimer on screen explains that the host was paid to sell the face masks.
wrong3: The host speaks slowly and calmly, letting viewers decide quietly in their own time.

statement: This TV advert for the Ridgeback 4x4 shows a single driver crossing a huge, empty desert. There are no roads, only sand dunes, rocks and an enormous sky. The car climbs steep hills and races through a dry riverbed, sending up clouds of dust. At night, the driver sleeps on the roof under the stars. We never see a city, a road sign or another person during the whole advert. The strapline appears at the end: "Ridgeback. Go where the road ends." The advert appears during adventure and wildlife documentaries.
right1: Targeting people who love adventure and freedom is psychographics, not just age or income.
right2: The empty desert and night on the roof sell an adventurous lifestyle, not just a car.
right3: Showing it during adventure documentaries reaches viewers who already enjoy wild, remote places.
wrong1: The strapline is a disclaimer warning drivers not to leave the road in a 4x4.
wrong2: Body copy compares fuel costs with other cars, giving viewers a strong rational appeal.
wrong3: City streets and traffic jams show the car is perfect for daily school runs.

statement: Above a busy crossing in a large city, a giant curved screen shows a 3D image of a huge orange cartoon cat. Because of the shape of the screen, the cat appears to climb out of the building and look down at the people below. It yawns, stretches and finally holds up a can of Purr cat food. There are no words or prices, only the brand's logo in the corner. People stop in the street to film it, and videos of the billboard have been shared millions of times.
right1: The surprising 3D effect makes people stop and film, turning the billboard into viral marketing.
right2: With no words or prices, the giant cat is a soft sell that entertains first.
right3: The cat holding the can at the end links the brand with fun and surprise.
wrong1: The billboard is targeted advertising, because it only appears on the phones of cat owners nearby.
wrong2: A countdown on the screen creates scarcity, warning that the cat food is almost sold out.
wrong3: Most people walk past without looking up, so the billboard gets very little attention.

statement: This poster for the Run Club sportswatch shows a woman running alone along an empty city street in heavy rain. She is soaking wet, but her face is calm and focused. On her wrist, the small watch screen is glowing bright green. The photo is dark, with grey and blue tones. The only words are "Your pace." in small white letters in the top corner, and the brand's logo below. The poster appears in train stations in the early morning, when tired commuters walk past on the way to work.
right1: The words "Your pace." act as anchorage, telling us the run is personal, not a race.
right2: Running alone in heavy rain shows determination, linking the watch with people who never give up.
right3: Placing it in stations early in the morning reaches commuters who might wish they were running.
wrong1: The advert is a hard sell, using loud offers and prices to push tired commuters into buying.
wrong2: Body copy explains the watch's battery life, GPS and heart-rate features in clear detail.
wrong3: The bright, sunny colours of the photo make running feel light, easy and relaxing.

statement: This full-page magazine advert for Northern Oil is dominated by green. A row of white wind turbines stands on a hillside covered in fresh grass, and in the foreground, a child's hand holds a single bright green leaf. The headline reads, "Powering a cleaner tomorrow." The body copy describes the company's investment in renewable energy, using words such as "natural", "responsible" and "future". Only one line, near the end, mentions that solar and wind make up less than three per cent of the company's business. The company's logo, a green and yellow sunflower, sits quietly in the bottom right corner.
right1: The green imagery is greenwashing, since renewables make up under three per cent of the business.
right2: The green leaf and sunflower act as signifiers, making readers think of nature rather than oil.
right3: Words like "natural" and "responsible" in the body copy hide the scale of the company's real activity.
wrong1: The child's hand is a parody of old oil adverts, mocking the industry from within.
wrong2: A disclaimer in bold type admits that most of the company's profits still come from oil.
wrong3: Putting the three per cent figure in the headline shows the company is being completely transparent.

statement: This poster appeared overnight on a busy bus shelter in central London. At first glance, it looks exactly like an advert for Tasty Burger, with the same red background, the same smiling logo and the same photograph of a huge, dripping cheeseburger. However, the slogan has been changed from "Grab some happy" to "Grab some heart disease". Underneath, in the brand's own font, a line of small print lists the burger's salt, sugar and fat content. The poster was made by an activist group, not the company, and photos of it spread quickly across social media within a single day.
right1: Copying the brand's red background, logo and photo is subvertising that turns the advert against itself.
right2: Changing "happy" to "heart disease" is a parody that exposes what the original slogan hides.
right3: Using the brand's own font for the nutrition facts makes the criticism look official and believable.
wrong1: The poster is a pastiche, copying the brand's style respectfully to celebrate its long history.
wrong2: A countdown in the corner warns readers that the burger offer ends at midnight tonight.
wrong3: Tasty Burger made the poster itself, using honest humour to build trust with health-conscious customers.

statement: This thirty-second TV advert for the Robo mop opens with a loud crash as a toddler knocks a bowl of cereal onto a clean white kitchen floor. The parents look at each other in complete despair. A voiceover asks, "Tired of cleaning the same floor three times a day?" Next, the Robo mop glides out from under a cupboard and cleans the mess in seconds while the family sit down to breakfast. The voiceover lists three features: it maps the room, it empties itself and it is controlled by a phone app. The final screen says, "Order now. Delivery tomorrow."
right1: The crash grabs attention, the question builds interest, and the features create desire, following the AIDA model.
right2: The final screen's imperatives provide the action stage, making ordering feel quick, simple and immediate.
right3: Listing three features gives a rational appeal after the emotional, chaotic opening with the toddler.
wrong1: The cereal crash is an example of intertextuality, because it recreates the opening of a horror film.
wrong2: The final screen offers delivery next week, so the action stage feels slow and unconvincing.
wrong3: The advert opens with the order button, so the action stage comes before attention and interest.

statement: This TV advert for Volley sportswear follows a girls' under-fifteen football team through a muddy, rainy season. We see them training in the dark, arguing with referees and celebrating a very late winning goal. At the beginning, a boy on the touchline shouts, "You play like a girl!" as an insult. At the end, the team captain turns to the camera after scoring and repeats the phrase proudly: "Yeah. I play like a girl." The Volley logo appears on the team's shirts throughout, and the final screen shows the hashtag #LikeAGirl next to a link to the new women's collection.
right1: Reclaiming "like a girl" as praise is femvertising that challenges a common insult about girls' sporting ability.
right2: Showing mud, rain and arguments presents girls' football as serious, demanding and tough, not decorative.
right3: Linking the hashtag to the women's collection shows the empowering message also serves to sell clothes.
wrong1: The boy's insult is greenwashing, because it hides the brand's poor treatment of factory workers.
wrong2: A famous male footballer's voiceover explains why girls deserve the same respect and pay as boys.
wrong3: The girls are shown in perfect kit and slow motion, presenting them as graceful rather than strong.

statement: This TV advert for the new Kite phone uses a split screen. On the left, a young man struggles with last year's Kite 7 model: the screen is dull, apps load slowly and the battery runs out during a video call. The colours on that side are grey and washed out. On the right, a confident young woman uses the new model, which is bright, fast and full of colour, as she films a crowded outdoor concert. A voiceover says, "Why live in the past?" The final screen shows the new phone next to a trade-in offer for older models.
right1: Making last year's model look grey and slow encourages planned obsolescence, pushing owners to upgrade early.
right2: The split screen links the new phone with confidence and colour, and the old one with failure.
right3: "Why live in the past?" turns owning an older phone into something faintly embarrassing for viewers.
wrong1: The split screen is a pastiche of a 1950s film, using black and white to suggest nostalgia.
wrong2: A disclaimer explains that the old phone's software will stop receiving security updates next month.
wrong3: The old model is shown working perfectly, suggesting customers should keep their phones for longer.

statement: This magazine advert for Aurum shows a long dinner table in an elegant restaurant, lit by candles. Eight well-dressed guests in their thirties are laughing and talking. In the centre of the image, a man reaches for his wine glass, and his heavy gold watch catches the light. Several guests are glancing at it. The man's face is not fully shown, so the watch is the real subject of the photograph. The text is minimal: "Aurum. Noticed." There is no price and no information about the watch's features, only the brand name and the address of its single London boutique.
right1: Guests glancing at the watch show conspicuous consumption: its value lies partly in being seen.
right2: Hiding the man's face makes the watch the subject, so it signifies status rather than personality.
right3: The single word "Noticed." suggests the purpose of owning the watch is other people's attention.
wrong1: The candlelit table is greenwashing, suggesting the watch is made entirely from recycled and natural materials.
wrong2: The body copy explains the watch's mechanism and the years of craft behind each piece.
wrong3: The watch is hidden under his sleeve, suggesting real luxury is private and never shown off.

statement: This online advert for Peak Air shows a small aluminium can with a picture of snowy mountains on the side. A young woman in a crowded, polluted city lifts the can to her face, presses a button and breathes in deeply. Her eyes close in pleasure, and she smiles slowly. The text describes the product as "100% pure Alpine air, hand-collected at 3,000 metres". It claims the air will leave buyers feeling "refreshed, focused and alive". Each can contains about one hundred breaths and costs £14.99. The advert appears on social media in cities with high levels of air pollution.
right1: Selling air in cans is commodification, turning something free and natural into a product with a price.
right2: Phrases like "hand-collected at 3,000 metres" are puffery that make ordinary air sound rare and precious.
right3: Targeting polluted cities sells a feeling of escape to people who cannot easily reach clean air.
wrong1: The snowy mountains are planned obsolescence, because the can is designed to stop working quickly.
wrong2: A scientific study quoted in the advert proves that canned air improves concentration at work.
wrong3: The advert admits the air is ordinary, so customers know exactly what they are paying for.

statement: This TV advert for Lumi perfume is filmed entirely in black and white, in the style of a 1950s Hollywood film. A woman in a long satin dress and white gloves walks slowly down a grand marble staircase as an orchestra plays dramatic music. Men in dinner suits turn to watch her. The credits at the beginning use old-fashioned curly lettering, and the picture even has small scratches, as if it were an old film reel. In the final seconds, the bottle of Lumi appears in full colour, glowing gold, while the rest of the screen stays black and white.
right1: Imitating a 1950s Hollywood film is pastiche, borrowing old-fashioned glamour and style without mocking it.
right2: The fake scratches and curly lettering are details that create nostalgia for a lost golden age.
right3: Showing only the bottle in colour makes the perfume the one modern, living thing on screen.
wrong1: The black-and-white style is a parody that mocks old Hollywood films and the people who loved them.
wrong2: The voiceover lists the perfume's ingredients, giving viewers a clear, rational reason to buy it.
wrong3: The bottle appears in black and white like everything else, so it blends into the old film.

statement: This TV advert for Homeguard alarm systems shows a family's house at night, seen from outside. Rain is falling, and a heavy storm is building. Inside, the parents check on their sleeping children before going to bed themselves. A small blue light glows steadily on a white box by the front door. A calm, reassuring voiceover says, "Whatever happens outside, they're safe inside." The camera then shows a phone screen, where the parents can watch every room. The advert ends with the family having breakfast together in a bright kitchen and the strapline, "Homeguard. Peace of mind, around the clock."
right1: The advert targets the need for safety in Maslow's hierarchy of needs, especially parents protecting children.
right2: The storm outside contrasts with the calm house, suggesting the alarm keeps every danger out.
right3: The blue light acts as a signifier of protection, quietly watching over the sleeping family all night.
wrong1: The advert appeals mainly to self-actualisation, showing the parents reaching their full creative potential through art.
wrong2: A burglar breaking a window creates a strong fear appeal before the alarm saves the family.
wrong3: The family looks frightened at breakfast, suggesting the alarm has not made them feel safe.

statement: This online advert for Kingdom Clash does not show the game itself for most of its thirty seconds. Instead, it shows four teenage friends in different cities, each in their own bedroom, talking and laughing on a video call while they play together. One friend has just moved to a new country, and the others greet her with cheers when she joins their team. They share inside jokes and call each other by nicknames that only they understand. Only at the end does the advert show the game's colourful battle screen, followed by the line, "Wherever you are, play together."
right1: The advert sells the game through uses and gratifications, especially the need for social interaction with friends.
right2: Hiding the gameplay until the end suggests friendship, not fighting, is the real product.
right3: The friend who has moved abroad shows the game keeping relationships alive across countries and distance.
wrong1: The video call is a dark pattern, tricking players into spending money they did not intend.
wrong2: A countdown offers new players a pack of free gems for the first twenty-four hours only.
wrong3: Each teenager plays alone in silence, presenting gaming as a way to escape from other people.

statement: When readers try to leave the website of a popular food magazine, a large pop-up suddenly fills the screen. It offers a subscription at £1 for the first month. The "Subscribe" button is large, bright green and in the centre of the box. Underneath, in small grey text, the option to close the pop-up says, "No thanks, I don't like saving money." Next to the green button, a small box has already been ticked for them to agree to marketing emails. In the small print, readers can see that after the first month the price rises to £12 a month.
right1: "No thanks, I don't like saving money" is a dark pattern that makes refusing feel foolish.
right2: The pre-ticked marketing box is another dark pattern, collecting consent that people never actively gave.
right3: Making "Subscribe" large and green while "close" is small and grey steers users towards one choice.
wrong1: The £1 offer is puffery, a vague boast that no reader could check or measure.
wrong2: The subscription costs £12 for the first month, then falls to £1, which rewards loyal readers.
wrong3: The close option is the largest button, so leaving the website is easy and pressure-free.

statement: This billboard for Bean There coffee shows a close-up of a cup of coffee on a wooden table, with steam rising and a perfect heart drawn in the milk foam. Dark roasted coffee beans are scattered around the cup, and a small chocolate sits on the saucer. Across the top, in large, elegant cream letters, the billboard claims, "The best coffee in the world." There is no evidence, award or statistic to support the claim. Underneath, a smaller line reads, "Now in over 400 cafés." The billboard is placed directly opposite a rival coffee chain on a busy shopping street.
right1: "The best coffee in the world" is puffery, a vague boast that nobody could prove or disprove.
right2: Placing it opposite a rival chain turns the claim into a direct challenge to competitors.
right3: The heart in the milk foam is a signifier of care, love and skilled craft from baristas.
wrong1: "Now in over 400 cafés" is puffery, because it is impossible to count the cafés.
wrong2: A blind taste test quoted on the billboard supports the claim with clear, independent evidence.
wrong3: The billboard is placed far from any rival café, avoiding direct competition on the street.

statement: This magazine advert for Starlight jewellers shows a dark wooden table lit only by a single candle. On the table, there is a single deep red rose and a small open box containing a diamond ring. A few rose petals lie beside it, and a glass of champagne stands in the shadows behind. The image is warm and slightly blurred at the edges, so the ring is the sharpest object in the picture. There are no people and no words except the brand's name, written in thin silver handwriting at the bottom, and the date of Valentine's Day, 14 February.
right1: The red rose, candle and champagne are signifiers whose signified meaning is romance and commitment.
right2: Blurring the edges makes the ring the sharpest object, guiding the reader's eye to it.
right3: Printing the date of Valentine's Day anchors the image to one occasion and creates urgency.
wrong1: The ring is the signified, while romance is the signifier that the reader sees on the table.
wrong2: A couple kissing in the background shows readers the happy moment just after the proposal.
wrong3: Bright, harsh lighting makes the scene feel clinical, as if the ring were a scientific object.

statement: Across a whole year of TV adverts, Hollins supermarket always uses the same family. The parents are white and in their forties, with two children, a boy and a girl, and a golden retriever. They live in a large detached house with a big garden in the countryside. The mother is usually cooking, while the father lights the barbecue or carves the meat. They are always calm and well-dressed, they never argue, and their huge kitchen is spotless and full of expensive equipment. Each advert ends with the family around the table and the strapline, "Hollins. Food for every family."
right1: Using the same wealthy white family reinforces hegemony, presenting one kind of family as normal.
right2: The mother cooking while the father carves the meat repeats traditional gender roles from older adverts.
right3: "Food for every family" contrasts with the narrow, idealised family that the adverts actually show every time.
wrong1: The family's detached house is an example of femvertising that challenges gender stereotypes about mothers.
wrong2: Price comparisons with other supermarkets give the adverts a strong rational appeal for families.
wrong3: Each advert shows a different kind of family, so viewers from many backgrounds feel included.

statement: This billboard originally advertised a huge three-day weekend sale at a shopping centre, with the headline "Buy more. Save more." and a photograph of smiling shoppers carrying bags. During the night, however, someone painted over two words, so that it now reads "Buy more. Be happy?" A large red question mark has been added beside the shoppers' smiling faces. The change was made by an anti-consumerism group, who also attached small stickers reading "Buy Nothing Day" around the frame. Photos of the altered billboard were shared thousands of times online before the shopping centre had it cleaned the next afternoon.
right1: Repainting the billboard is culture jamming, using the advert's own space to question its message.
right2: Turning "Save more" into "Be happy?" challenges the consumerist idea that buying more brings happiness.
right3: Leaving the smiling shoppers in place makes their happiness look empty once the question is added.
wrong1: The repainted billboard is a pastiche, celebrating the shopping centre's style with warmth and affection.
wrong2: The activists added a QR code linking to a website where people can buy cheaper clothes.
wrong3: The shopping centre paid for the change, using humour to make shoppers trust the sale more.

statement: This TV advert for Rocket crisps retells the story of Little Red Riding Hood. A girl in a red cloak walks through a dark, misty forest, carrying a basket of food for her sick grandmother. When she reaches her grandmother's cottage, the wolf is in the bed, wearing a nightdress. However, when she says, "What big teeth you have!", the wolf ignores her and grabs the bag of Rocket crisps from her basket. He eats them noisily and happily and says, "Sorry, I'm not here for you." The advert ends with a packshot and the line, "Rocket. Worth the trip."
right1: Retelling Little Red Riding Hood uses intertextuality, relying on viewers already knowing how the story goes.
right2: Changing the wolf's goal from the girl to the crisps parodies the tale for comic effect.
right3: The tagline's pun on "trip" connects the forest journey with the crisps being worth it.
wrong1: The fairy tale is greenwashing, using a forest setting to make the crisps seem environmentally friendly.
wrong2: A voiceover lists the crisps' new lower salt content, giving parents a healthy reason to buy.
wrong3: The story follows the original exactly, with no surprise, so the brand appears serious and traditional.

statement: This TV advert for ValueMart's Black Friday sale begins with a crowd of people waiting outside a large store in the dark. A large digital clock counts down the final seconds to midnight. When the doors open, the shoppers rush inside, grabbing televisions, laptops and toys from the shelves. Loud, upbeat music plays, and the editing is fast and exciting. Prices with red lines through them flash across the screen, replaced by lower ones. The voiceover shouts, "Biggest deals of the year! Once they're gone, they're gone!" The advert ends with smiling customers carrying huge cardboard boxes to their cars.
right1: Shoppers rushing and grabbing goods celebrate consumerism, presenting buying as exciting and joyful rather than necessary.
right2: "Once they're gone, they're gone!" creates scarcity, so viewers fear missing out on the year's bargains.
right3: The fast editing and loud music turn shopping into an exciting event, encouraging quick impulse buys.
wrong1: The countdown clock is a pastiche of a 1920s silent film, adding old-fashioned charm.
wrong2: A disclaimer warns viewers that many of the lowest prices apply to only a few items.
wrong3: The slow, calm shoppers suggest ValueMart encourages people to think carefully before buying anything.

statement: This online advert for Trendy's new "Conscious Collection" shows models in soft beige and green clothes walking through a sunny field of tall wild flowers. Leaves and small birds appear in the corners of the screen. Calm, elegant text across the screen says, "Fashion that cares for the planet." The collection is presented on a special green page of the website, with a leaf symbol beside each item. However, the product labels show that most items contain only 1% recycled cotton. The rest of the website continues to sell hundreds of brand new styles every week at very low prices.
right1: Calling clothes with 1% recycled cotton "conscious" is greenwashing that greatly exaggerates the brand's environmental care.
right2: Leaves, birds and wild flowers are signifiers of nature that hide a fast fashion business.
right3: Hundreds of new styles every week contradict the message that the brand cares for the planet.
wrong1: The wild flowers are planned obsolescence, because the clothes are designed to fall apart quickly.
wrong2: An independent certificate on the green page proves that the whole collection is fully sustainable.
wrong3: The labels show the clothes are 100% recycled, so the claim about the planet is honest.

statement: This TV advert for the Ridgeback SUV shows a large black car driving slowly down a busy, narrow city street. People on the pavement stop and turn to look at it. A group of young men nod in admiration, and a woman in a café smiles at the driver through the window. The driver, a man in his forties wearing dark sunglasses, parks in front of an expensive restaurant, and the doorman opens his door. The car never leaves the city, drives on rough ground or carries anything heavier than a shopping bag. The strapline appears: "Ridgeback. Make an entrance."
right1: People admiring the car show conspicuous consumption: its value lies in being seen, not used.
right2: The doorman and expensive restaurant appeal to the esteem needs in Maslow's hierarchy of needs.
right3: Never going off-road suggests the 4x4 is a status symbol, not a practical vehicle.
wrong1: The admiring crowd is femvertising, presenting women as powerful drivers in control of the city.
wrong2: Body copy explains the car's off-road features, giving buyers a rational reason to choose it.
wrong3: Nobody on the street notices the car, suggesting it is modest and practical rather than showy.

statement: This online advert for the Spark dating app shows a series of short scenes of young people getting ready to go out: choosing clothes, practising a smile in the mirror, and taking a deep breath before entering a bar. Each person looks nervous and unsure at first, but calm and confident by the end of the scene. A voiceover says, "Be the person you want to be. Spark will help you find someone who loves them." Users' profile photos appear on screen, with descriptions such as "adventurous" and "creative". The advert ends with the line, "Your best self is waiting."
right1: The app sells uses and gratifications linked to personal identity, offering users a better version of themselves.
right2: Moving from nervous to confident suggests the app can solve social anxiety, not just loneliness.
right3: Profile words like "adventurous" turn personalities into labels, a kind of commodification of people and relationships.
wrong1: The scenes of getting ready are greenwashing, presenting the app as environmentally responsible and natural.
wrong2: Testimonials from married couples on screen prove that the app leads to long, happy relationships.
wrong3: Each person becomes more nervous by the end, so the app seems to make dating harder.

statement: In a long corridor at a busy metro station, Fairway Bank has placed four posters in a row. The first shows only a large question: "Still paying bank fees?" The second shows a frustrated young woman looking at a bank charge on her phone. The third explains, in a few short lines, that Fairway's new account has no fees and pays interest every month. The fourth shows the same woman smiling, with the words, "Switch in ten minutes. Scan here." Each poster uses the same yellow background, and commuters see all four in order as they walk to the platform.
right1: The four posters follow the AIDA model, moving commuters from attention to action as they walk.
right2: The frustrated woman with a bank charge makes the problem personal before the solution appears.
right3: Ending with "Scan here" gives a simple, immediate action at the exact moment of greatest interest.
wrong1: The corridor is culture jamming, because activists have changed the bank's posters to criticise it.
wrong2: The second poster shows a smiling woman, so the problem is never made to feel personal.
wrong3: The posters are randomly placed, so commuters see the action stage before understanding the problem.

statement: This TV advert for Edge's women's razors shows women of different ages, ethnicities and body shapes at the beach, at the gym and in the bathroom. Unlike most razor adverts, it shows real, natural body hair on legs, arms and underarms. Some women shave, while others choose not to, and neither choice is shown as better. A voiceover says, "Your body. Your choice. No judgement." There is no slow motion, no perfect lighting and no models with already smooth legs. The final screen shows the razor in simple pink and grey packaging, alongside the words, "Edge. For whatever you decide."
right1: Showing real, natural body hair is femvertising that challenges the idealised images in most razor adverts.
right2: Saying neither choice is better presents the razor as optional, which feels respectful to viewers.
right3: There is still a tension, because the advert uses a feminist message to sell razors.
wrong1: Including women of different ages is hegemony, because it supports the most powerful group's values.
wrong2: A famous model with perfectly smooth legs appears at the end to show the razor's results.
wrong3: Slow motion and perfect lighting present the women as flawless, like the models in traditional razor adverts.

statement: This TV advert for Homeguard insurance is filmed like a trailer for a superhero film. Loud, dramatic orchestral music builds, and a deep voice says, "In a world of burst pipes and broken windows, one hero stands ready." A man in an ordinary grey suit, holding a clipboard, walks in slow motion away from a small kitchen flood while sparks fly behind him. He arrives at a family's door and says, "Don't worry, I'm from Homeguard." The title appears in huge metal letters: "HOMEGUARD: THE CLAIM." The advert ends with the company's website and a phone number for making claims.
right1: Filming insurance like a superhero trailer is parody, mocking the genre's drama for comic effect.
right2: The ordinary man with a clipboard contrasts humorously with the epic music and slow motion.
right3: This intertextuality relies on viewers recognising film trailer conventions, such as the line "In a world...".
wrong1: The trailer is a pastiche that copies superhero films seriously and respectfully, without any humour or exaggeration.
wrong2: A disclaimer warns that claims for small floods may take several months to be paid.
wrong3: The flood is shown as a terrifying disaster, using a serious fear appeal to frighten families.

statement: This online advert for the Pulse smartwatch shows a woman sleeping, running and working at a desk, while numbers and graphs float around her body. Her heart rate, sleep score, steps and stress level are all displayed in bright blue. Each number changes constantly, even while she is asleep or eating breakfast. At one point, a message appears on the watch: "Your recovery score is low. Rest today." The strapline appears in clean white letters: "Your body, measured." At the end, the advert says the watch comes with a free month of Pulse Premium, which then costs £8 a month.
right1: "Your body, measured" turns health into data, a commodification of the body and of daily life.
right2: Numbers changing even while she sleeps suggest the watch never stops watching or judging her.
right3: The free month leads into a monthly fee, so the watch also sells a subscription.
wrong1: The bright blue numbers are pastiche, imitating the look of 1980s science fiction films.
wrong2: A doctor's testimonial explains that the watch can diagnose serious illnesses early and accurately.
wrong3: The watch only shows the time, presenting it as simple and free from constant data.

statement: This online advert for the Jet 200 printer shows the small white machine on a tidy desk beside a laptop and a small green plant. Large blue letters announce, "Only £30!" Below, three smiling students happily print bright, colourful posters for a school science project. However, the product page explains in small print that the printer only works with official Jet ink cartridges, which cost £40 for a set. It also says that cartridges from other brands will be blocked by a chip inside the printer. At the bottom, the advert also offers an "ink subscription" for £6 a month.
right1: The cheap printer and expensive ink suggest the real profit comes from cartridges, not the machine.
right2: Blocking other brands' cartridges with a chip limits consumer choice and locks buyers in for years.
right3: Hiding the ink rules in small print on the product page makes "Only £30!" misleading.
wrong1: The smiling students are an example of conspicuous consumption, showing off expensive goods to others.
wrong2: A disclaimer warns that the printer will stop working after exactly two years of use.
wrong3: The printer works with any cartridge, giving customers freedom to choose the cheapest ink.

statement: This TV advert for a Chinese supermarket chain shows a young woman travelling home from a big city on the night before Chinese New Year. Through the train window, red lanterns glow in every village. When she arrives, her grandmother is making dumplings at the kitchen table, and a whole steamed fish is being prepared for dinner. The room is filled with red decorations and paper cuttings of the character for "fortune". The family eat together as fireworks explode outside. The advert ends with the supermarket's logo and a short, gentle line in gold: "Home is where the table is."
right1: Red lanterns, the whole fish and the character for "fortune" are signifiers of luck and togetherness.
right2: The long journey home creates nostalgia and emotional appeal for viewers who live far from family.
right3: The final line connects the supermarket with reunion, so buying food becomes an act of love.
wrong1: The fireworks are greenwashing, suggesting the supermarket is environmentally responsible and green during the busy festival.
wrong2: Price tags on the dumplings and fish give viewers a rational reason to shop there.
wrong3: The young woman stays alone in the city, suggesting modern life has replaced family traditions.

statement: In this online video, a popular fashion influencer sits on her bed surrounded by bright paper bags from Trendy. She takes out twenty items one by one, holding each one up to the camera and saying how cheap it was. "This top was only six pounds!" she says excitedly, laughing. Many of the items still have their price tags. She tries a few on and spins around happily in front of a mirror. In the caption, she lists every item with a link and a discount code. The video ends with her saying, "I'll be doing another haul next month!"
right1: Buying twenty items at once celebrates materialism, suggesting happiness comes from owning more and more things.
right2: Repeating how cheap each item was encourages viewers to see clothes as cheap and disposable.
right3: Promising another haul next month makes constant buying feel normal, fun and exciting for followers.
wrong1: The haul is subvertising, because the influencer is secretly criticising Trendy and the fast fashion industry.
wrong2: A disclaimer at the start explains that Trendy paid for every item in the video.
wrong3: She returns most of the items, suggesting viewers should buy less and choose carefully.

statement: This online advert for SkyHop shows a plane flying through a clear blue sky above a thick green forest. The plane's tail is painted with a large green leaf. The headline says, "Fly carbon neutral with SkyHop." Below, smaller text explains that for an extra £3 per ticket, the airline will plant trees in Scotland to "balance" the carbon from each flight. A disclaimer at the bottom of the page says that the trees will take up to forty years to absorb the carbon. The advert gives no information about how much fuel the planes actually burn on each journey.
right1: Calling flights "carbon neutral" while the trees take forty years to absorb carbon is greenwashing.
right2: The green leaf on the tail is a signifier of nature attached to a polluting product.
right3: Putting the forty-year detail in a disclaimer hides the main weakness in the headline's bold claim.
wrong1: The leaf on the tail is pastiche, imitating the style of 1950s travel posters.
wrong2: A chart comparing fuel use with other airlines proves SkyHop is the cleanest choice.
wrong3: The disclaimer says the trees absorb all the carbon immediately, so the claim is fully honest.

statement: In the mobile game Kingdom Clash, a pop-up advert appears while players are in the middle of a battle. It shows a glowing golden chest that shakes, sparkles and flashes with coloured light, while exciting music plays. Text says, "Legendary skins: only available for 24 hours!" A countdown timer runs beside the chest. Players cannot see what is inside until they buy it with gems, which cost real money. A small line says the chance of finding a legendary item is two per cent. The game is rated suitable for players aged twelve and over, and most players are teenagers.
right1: Flashing lights, a countdown and hidden contents are dark patterns that push players to spend.
right2: "Only available for 24 hours" creates scarcity, so players fear losing a rare chance forever.
right3: Showing the two per cent chance in a small line hides how unlikely winning really is.
wrong1: The glowing golden chest is femvertising, challenging traditional stereotypes about girls, boys and video gaming.
wrong2: A warning appears before every purchase, reminding teenagers to ask a parent for permission first.
wrong3: Players can see exactly what is inside before paying, so the chest feels fair and transparent.

statement: This online advert for Bean There coffee is made in the style of a 1920s silent film. It is in black and white, the picture is slightly shaky, and a piano plays quick, comic music. A tired man in a black bowler hat falls asleep at his desk, then wakes up and runs through the city, dodging cars and policemen, until he reaches a Bean There café. Old-fashioned title cards appear between scenes, such as "Mr Jones needed his coffee." When he finally takes his first sip, the whole screen bursts into full colour, and modern music begins to play.
right1: Copying a 1920s silent film is pastiche, using old-fashioned style affectionately to create humour and charm.
right2: The switch from black and white to colour signifies the coffee bringing him back to life.
right3: Title cards and comic chase scenes rely on intertextuality with early comedy films that many viewers know.
wrong1: The silent film style is subvertising, attacking the coffee brand by copying its own adverts.
wrong2: A voiceover explains where the beans come from and how they are carefully roasted in Italy.
wrong3: The whole advert stays in colour, so the first sip changes nothing on screen.

statement: This TV advert for the Volta car shows the car driving alone along a long, empty road through wide, green mountain valleys. There are no other vehicles, no buildings and no traffic lights. The sky is huge and blue, and the road disappears into the distance. The driver opens the window and puts her hand out into the wind. For a moment, a large eagle flies beside the car, level with the window. The only sound is quiet music and the wind. The final shot shows the car on a cliff edge at sunset, with the words, "Volta. Go further."
right1: The empty road, eagle and open window are signifiers whose shared signified meaning is freedom and escape.
right2: Removing traffic and buildings presents an idealised drive that few real owners will ever experience.
right3: This is lifestyle advertising: the car sells a feeling of escape more than a way of travelling.
wrong1: The eagle is the signified, while freedom is the signifier that the viewer sees on screen.
wrong2: Body copy lists the car's range, charging time and price for practical, careful buyers.
wrong3: Busy traffic and road signs present the car as a sensible choice for city commuters.

statement: This Christmas advert for Hollins supermarket shows a mother preparing the family's Christmas dinner from early morning. She peels potatoes, stuffs the turkey and makes the sauce while her husband and children play noisy board games and watch television in the next room. When the meal is ready, everyone sits down and applauds her loudly. She smiles proudly and says, "It's worth it to see their faces." Warm music plays throughout, and the kitchen is full of steam. The strapline appears at the end: "Hollins. Making Christmas magic, together." In the advert, the father carries the turkey to the table.
right1: The mother cooking while others relax reinforces hegemony, presenting unequal gender roles as natural and happy.
right2: Applause and "It's worth it" turn her unpaid work into a reward rather than a problem.
right3: The father carrying the turkey takes the moment of glory after she does the work.
wrong1: The advert is femvertising, because it challenges the stereotype that women should do the cooking.
wrong2: Price labels on the food give families a rational appeal based on saving money this Christmas.
wrong3: The whole family cooks together all morning, so the strapline's "together" is completely accurate.

statement: This poster by a charity that campaigns for factory workers' rights looks almost exactly like a luxury advert for Maison Noir handbags. It uses the same plain white background, the same elegant gold font and the same type of large, glossy photograph. However, instead of a model, the person holding the handbag is a tired young woman in a factory, surrounded by rows of sewing machines. The slogan has been changed from "Only 100 made" to "Made by hands you'll never see." At the bottom, a line says that the worker earned less than the cost of the bag's zip.
right1: Copying the luxury style to show the factory worker is subvertising, using the brand's look against it.
right2: Changing "Only 100 made" to "Made by hands you'll never see" exposes what luxury adverts hide.
right3: Comparing her pay with the zip's cost shows the product as a commodity built on cheap labour.
wrong1: The poster is a pastiche, admiring the handbag brand and imitating it to celebrate its success.
wrong2: Maison Noir's response is printed at the bottom, explaining how it treats factory workers fairly.
wrong3: The model holding the bag looks relaxed and glamorous, so the poster celebrates luxury fashion.

statement: This social media advert for Bliss bath bombs shows a young woman sinking into a bath full of pink and purple bubbles. Candles are burning around the bath, and her phone is switched off on a towel. Soft piano music plays, and she closes her eyes. The caption says, "You deserve this. Self-care starts at £6." Below, a voiceover says, "Because looking after yourself isn't selfish." The advert offers a box of twelve bath bombs as a "self-care subscription" that arrives every month. It appears mainly on Sunday evenings, when many young people are feeling stressed about the week ahead.
right1: Selling self-care as a monthly subscription is commodification, turning rest and relaxation into something you buy.
right2: "You deserve this" uses direct address to give viewers permission to spend money on themselves.
right3: Appearing on Sunday evenings targets stressed young people when their need for comfort is strongest.
wrong1: The candles and bubbles are greenwashing, presenting the bath bombs as natural and environmentally friendly.
wrong2: A dermatologist's testimonial explains that the bath bombs are safe for sensitive or dry skin.
wrong3: Her phone is on and buzzing, suggesting she can never truly switch off and relax.

statement: This streaming service has a homepage that automatically begins playing a trailer as soon as the user arrives. When an episode ends, the next one starts after just five seconds, with a countdown in the corner of the screen. The service describes itself as "endless stories for every mood". Cancelling the subscription requires the user to find a small link at the bottom of the account settings page, then answer three questions and click through two screens that ask, "Are you sure you want to miss out?" The free trial ends automatically after seven days, and payment begins without warning.
right1: Hiding the cancel link and adding questions are dark patterns that make leaving deliberately difficult.
right2: Autoplay after five seconds keeps viewers watching before they have consciously decided to continue.
right3: "Are you sure you want to miss out?" plays on the fear of missing out.
wrong1: The trailer on the homepage is culture jamming, criticising the service from inside its own website.
wrong2: A reminder email arrives three days before the trial ends, warning users that payment will begin.
wrong3: Cancelling takes one click from the homepage, showing the service respects users' choices.

statement: This billboard for Glacier water shows a plastic bottle standing on a large block of blue ice in front of snowy mountains. The bottle is clear and covered in cold drops of water, and the label is pale blue with a drawing of a mountain peak. The slogan says, "Pure as nature." In smaller letters, the billboard says, "Sourced from the Alps." There is no mention of the plastic bottle itself, what happens to it afterwards, or how far it travels to reach the shops. The billboard stands beside a motorway in a city two thousand kilometres from the Alps.
right1: "Pure as nature" connects a plastic product with nature, which is a form of greenwashing.
right2: The ice, mountains and pale blue label are signifiers of purity, freshness and cold.
right3: Leaving out the bottle's journey and waste hides the product's real environmental cost from readers.
wrong1: The mountain drawing is intertextuality, because it copies a well-known Japanese print of a wave.
wrong2: Small print at the bottom states that every bottle is made from 100% recycled plastic.
wrong3: The billboard openly shows the plastic waste, so readers understand the product's real impact.

statement: This TV advert for Volley sportswear follows a group of women in their seventies training for a marathon. They run together through a city park on cold, dark mornings, stretch on park benches and laugh about their sore knees and backs. One woman is seen collecting her granddaughter from school, still in her running clothes, with a medal around her neck. On race day, they cross the finish line together, holding hands. There are no young models in the advert. The final screen shows the women's ages, from 71 to 79, followed by the strapline, "Volley. Start whenever you want."
right1: Showing women in their seventies challenges the idea that sport belongs only to the young.
right2: Showing their ages on the final screen makes their achievement concrete, real and surprising.
right3: This is femvertising aimed at older women, positioning the brand as inclusive and encouraging for everyone.
wrong1: The women's sore knees are greenwashing, presenting the sportswear as natural and environmentally friendly.
wrong2: The final screen shows the women's ages, from 51 to 59, presenting them as middle-aged runners.
wrong3: Young models in perfect kit run past the older women, so age is presented as weakness.

statement: This poster for Kite phones shows an old, scratched phone lying in a museum display case, as if it were an ancient object. A small label beside it reads, "Kite 5, 2023." The lighting is dim, and the glass is slightly dusty. Next to the case, there is a photograph of the shiny, slim new Kite 8. The strapline says, "Your old phone is history." Below, smaller text offers up to £200 off when customers trade in their old phone. The poster appears in train stations and shopping centres across the country, two years after the Kite 5 was released.
right1: Putting a two-year-old phone in a museum encourages planned obsolescence, making recent technology seem ancient.
right2: The dusty, dim case contrasts with the shiny new phone, signifying the gap between old and modern.
right3: "Your old phone is history" is a pun that mocks owners for keeping their phones too long.
wrong1: The museum case is subvertising, created by activists to criticise how quickly phones are replaced.
wrong2: Body copy explains that old phones are recycled responsibly when customers trade them in at the shop.
wrong3: The old phone is shown working perfectly, encouraging people to keep it for many more years.

statement: This magazine advert for Maison Noir shows a young woman walking out of a famous luxury hotel in Paris, carrying a handbag covered in the brand's own logo: a repeated pattern of two gold letters, M and N. Her clothes are simple and black, so the bag is the only thing with a pattern. On the street, a photographer is taking her picture, and two other women turn to look at the bag as she passes. The only text is the brand's name in thin gold letters. The bag costs £2,800, but the price is not shown in the advert.
right1: The logo pattern is conspicuous consumption, because the bag's main job is to be recognised.
right2: Two women turning to look show that owning the bag brings attention and social status.
right3: Plain black clothes make the logo the only pattern, so the brand becomes the message.
