wrong1: The repeated letters are puffery, a vague boast that the bag is the best in the world.
wrong2: Body copy describes the leather and stitching, giving readers a rational reason to pay £2,800.
wrong3: The logo is hidden inside the bag, suggesting true luxury is quiet and private.

statement: Every time a user opens the Bargain Hunt shopping app, a colourful prize wheel appears before they can see anything else. The wheel spins with flashing lights and cheerful sounds, and it always stops on a discount, such as 30% off, which is only valid for the next fifteen minutes. A countdown starts immediately. To close the wheel, the user must tap a tiny grey cross in the corner. Many of the discounts only apply if the user spends more than £40. Push notifications are sent to the user every evening, reminding them that their prizes are about to expire.
right1: The prize wheel and tiny close button are dark patterns that make ignoring the offer difficult.
right2: A fifteen-minute countdown creates scarcity, pushing users into quick impulse buys before thinking carefully.
right3: Making every spin win something turns shopping into a game and encourages users to return.
wrong1: The prize wheel is pastiche, imitating a 1920s silent film to give the app old-fashioned charm.
wrong2: A disclaimer explains how the app chooses discounts and how often users really win anything.
wrong3: The wheel only appears when users ask for it, so the app respects their time.

statement: This fifteen-second TV advert for Surge energy drink begins with a close-up of a student yawning at a library desk covered in books, notes and empty coffee cups. A deep voice says, "Exam season?" She opens a can of Surge, and electric blue lightning bolts suddenly appear around her head, while dramatic music starts. In seconds, she is typing at lightning speed, answering exam questions, and then running out of the exam hall with her arms in the air. The voice says, "Surge. Unleash your inner genius." The final frame shows the blue can and the words, "Grab yours today."
right1: In fifteen seconds the advert follows the AIDA model, from yawning attention to "Grab yours today".
right2: "Unleash your inner genius" is hyperbole that exaggerates what an ordinary energy drink can do.
right3: Lightning bolts signify sudden energy, linking the brand name Surge with power and speed.
wrong1: The library setting is an example of greenwashing, presenting the drink as natural and healthy.
wrong2: A disclaimer warns that the drink is not recommended for children or people sensitive to caffeine.
wrong3: The student stays tired and fails her exam, so the advert feels honest and realistic.

statement: This poster for Tasty Burger shows a famous Renaissance portrait of a woman with a mysterious smile. The painting looks exactly like the original, with the same dark background, soft light and folded hands. However, instead of resting her hands, she is now holding a large Tasty Burger, and a small amount of ketchup is on the side of her mouth. The caption says, "Now we know why she's smiling." The brand's logo appears once, in the corner, in the same gold as the old painting's frame. The poster is displayed in metro stations near the city's main art gallery.
right1: Changing the famous portrait into a burger advert is parody, playing with a well-known artwork.
right2: This intertextuality relies on viewers immediately recognising the famous painting and its mysterious smile.
right3: Placing it near the art gallery targets people who are most likely to get the joke.
wrong1: The poster is subvertising, created by activists to attack Tasty Burger using its own logo.
wrong2: Body copy explains the history of the painting and the artist who created it.
wrong3: The painting is changed so much that viewers cannot recognise it, which keeps the focus on food.

statement: This Christmas TV advert for a department store shows a family waking up on Christmas morning. The children run downstairs to find a huge, perfectly decorated tree surrounded by piles of beautifully wrapped presents. They open new phones, bikes, games consoles and designer clothes. Snow falls outside the window of their large, warm living room. Everyone is laughing and hugging, and nobody is shown without a gift. A voiceover says, "Give them the Christmas they deserve." The advert then shows a list of prices for each gift and offers a payment plan to "spread the cost into the new year".
right1: Piles of expensive presents link love and happiness with owning things, which suggests strong materialism.
right2: "Give them the Christmas they deserve" suggests parents who spend less are letting their children down.
right3: The payment plan encourages consumerism by making expensive gifts feel affordable now and painful later.
wrong1: The snowy window is intertextuality, recreating a scene from a well-known Christmas film.
wrong2: A small charity message reminds viewers to donate gifts to children who have nothing.
wrong3: The children receive one small, homemade present each, so the advert gently criticises materialism and spending.

statement: This online advert for the NowNews app shows a young man standing on a crowded metro carriage. While everyone around him looks bored or tired, his phone buzzes with a notification: "Breaking: election results in." He reads it quickly, smiles and puts his phone back in his pocket. Later, at work, his colleagues in the office are amazed that he already knows the news. The strapline appears on screen: "NowNews. Know first." The advert ends by explaining that the app sends alerts within seconds of a story breaking, and that users can choose topics such as sport, business and technology.
right1: In uses and gratifications terms, the app offers information, letting users feel informed before others.
right2: The colleagues' surprise shows that knowing the news first gives him status and respect at work.
right3: The bored passengers contrast with his smile, suggesting the app turns waiting time into something useful.
wrong1: The notification is a dark pattern that tricks him into paying for news he never chose.
wrong2: The notification is about a football result, presenting the app mainly as entertainment rather than information.
wrong3: He is the last to hear the news, so the app seems slow and unreliable.

statement: This poster for Bolt e-scooters shows a scooter parked on a city street that has been covered in green leaves and grass, like a forest. Bright flowers grow around the wheels, and butterflies and small birds fly above it in the sunshine. The headline says, "Zero emissions. Zero guilt." The colour palette is almost entirely green. Small white text at the very bottom says that the scooters produce no exhaust fumes. However, the poster does not mention the batteries, the diesel vans that collect and charge the scooters every night, or how long each scooter lasts before it is replaced.
right1: Covering the street in leaves and flowers is greenwashing that exaggerates the scooters' environmental benefits.
right2: "Zero guilt" suggests riders need not think about any environmental cost of their journey.
right3: Leaving out batteries and diesel vans hides the parts of the business that pollute.
wrong1: The butterflies are an example of hegemony, showing the powerful scooter company controlling all of nature.
wrong2: A full life-cycle study in the small print proves the scooters are better than walking.
wrong3: The poster openly mentions the diesel vans, showing the brand is honest about its pollution.

statement: On the busiest shopping day of the year, a group of about fifty ordinary-looking people enter a large, crowded shopping centre at midday. Suddenly, at exactly the same moment, they all freeze in place: some holding empty shopping bags, others with their hands reaching towards shop windows. They stay completely still for five minutes while shoppers stare and film them on their phones. Then they unfold banners that read, "Buy Nothing Day: what do you really need?" and walk out together in silence. Videos of the event are shared widely online, and several news websites report on it that evening.
right1: Freezing in the shopping centre is culture jamming that interrupts consumerism in its own busy space.
right2: Empty bags and reaching hands make the habits of shopping look strange, empty and automatic.
right3: The question "what do you really need?" challenges the materialism the shopping centre depends on.
wrong1: The flash mob is a pastiche, imitating an old shopping advert to celebrate the shopping centre.
wrong2: The group stays frozen for an hour, which turns the protest into a long, serious performance.
wrong3: The group buys something from every shop before leaving, supporting the shopping centre's sales.

statement: This online advert for the FitTrack fitness app shows a young woman running on a treadmill late at night, looking exhausted. On her phone screen, a picture of a pizza slowly appears as the calories she burns increase. When she reaches 800 calories, the pizza is complete, and a message says, "Well done! You've earned your dinner." The strapline appears: "FitTrack. Earn it." Every person who appears in the advert, including the people in the background of the gym, is very slim and toned. The advert ends with an offer of a free seven-day trial and then £9.99 a month.
right1: "Earn your dinner" turns food into a reward, commodifying eating as something to be paid for.
right2: Showing only slim, toned bodies presents an idealised body type as the normal and only goal.
right3: Her exhaustion late at night suggests exercise is punishment rather than enjoyment, fun or health.
wrong1: The pizza is intertextuality, because it recreates a scene from a television cookery competition.
wrong2: A nutritionist's testimonial explains why counting calories is a healthy daily habit for teenagers.
wrong3: People of all body types exercise happily, so the advert challenges idealised images of fitness.

statement: This social media post by an expensive restaurant in Shanghai shows a dish of tiny, colourful vegetables arranged like a painting on a large black plate. Small pieces of gold leaf have been placed on top, and a single flower lies at the edge of the plate. The photo is taken from directly above, with perfect lighting. A diner's hand holds a phone over the plate, ready to take a photograph. The caption says, "Made to be shared." The restaurant tags every customer who posts a photo of their meal and gives them a free dessert on their next visit.
right1: Gold leaf and painted vegetables make the dish a status symbol, an example of conspicuous consumption.
right2: The diner's phone over the plate suggests the meal is partly for showing others online.
right3: Free dessert for posting turns customers into advertisers, using their need for status and social recognition.
wrong1: The black plate is greenwashing, presenting the restaurant as environmentally responsible, local and sustainable.
wrong2: Body copy lists the price of the dish and the farm where each vegetable was grown.
wrong3: The photo is dark and casual, suggesting the dish is a simple everyday meal.

statement: This magazine advert for Purity water shows a tall, heavy glass bottle with a silver cap on a white marble table. Next to it, a single crystal glass is filled with water and a thin slice of lemon. The label describes the water as "carefully filtered and mineral-balanced for the modern palate". The bottle costs £8 in restaurants, where it is served by waiters in white gloves. In very small print at the bottom of the page, the advert admits that the water comes from the city's ordinary public water supply, which is then filtered and bottled in a factory.
right1: "Mineral-balanced for the modern palate" is puffery that makes ordinary filtered tap water sound special and rare.
right2: The heavy glass, marble and white gloves turn ordinary water into an expensive luxury commodity.
right3: Admitting the source only in very small print hides what customers are really paying for.
wrong1: The crystal glass is pastiche, copying the style of a 1950s Hollywood film for extra glamour.
wrong2: A blind taste test proves Purity tastes better than both tap water and other brands.
wrong3: The headline proudly says it is tap water, so customers know exactly what they are buying.

statement: This online advert for the Fairway Bank app looks like a video game from the 1980s. The graphics are made of large pixels, and a cheerful, simple electronic tune plays in the background. A small pixel character jumps over obstacles labelled "fees", "debt" and "paperwork", collecting gold coins as he runs. When he reaches the end of the level, the words "Savings unlocked!" flash on the screen. The final screen changes to a modern photograph of a smiling woman in her late thirties using the app on her phone. The music stops, and the advert ends with the bank's logo.
